tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.outcome: Take a real 'reachable for some clients, broken for others' incident (or a realistic one) and write a Path Trace: name the layer each symptom lives on — DNS, IP route, TLS trust, HTTP/proxy, or NetworkPolicy — and mark the ONE edge you suspect, before you touch application code.
tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.proof: Section 1 ('Path Trace') of network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md: the client→service path as ordered layers, the suspect layer marked, and at least two inspection-hook commands (dig / curl -v / openssl s_client / kubectl describe networkpolicy) named against the layers they interrogate. A reviewer can replay one hook and see what it would confirm or kill.
tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.unlock: Your Path Trace separates application symptoms from network causes, marks a suspect layer, and attaches a falsifiable inspection hook to it.
tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'traced the path' if your suspect is a guess with no command behind it. 'Probably DNS' is a hunch. The trace is proven only when a named hook (dig, curl -v, openssl s_client, kubectl describe networkpolicy) can return a 'no' and eliminate that layer.

tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.text: Half your users hit a clean 200; the other half get a spinner and a timeout. The room is three commits deep into the request handler — and the real fault is a stale DNS answer resolving to a decommissioned pod. Everyone is debugging the app. Nobody is tracing the path.

The TCP/IP model is not trivia to recite — it is the map you trace when a service is reachable from some clients and dead for others after a DNS, TLS, routing, or policy change. Its job is to tell application symptoms from network causes so you fix the layer that is actually broken.

tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.prompt: A service works from your laptop but 500s from inside the cluster after a deploy. First instinct: read the new application code? Decide before reading on.
tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.reveal: The split — works there, fails here — is the tell that the fault lives on the PATH, not in the handler. Same binary, same request, different network vantage: that isolates DNS resolution, route asymmetry, TLS trust, or a NetworkPolicy, not your business logic. Reading the code first debugs the one layer the evidence already cleared. Trace the path, and the 'works for some' pattern points straight at the broken edge.

tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.title: Trace the layer, don't debug the app
tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.text: Walk client → DNS → IP route → TLS trust → HTTP/proxy → NetworkPolicy in order, asking at each: does the symptom live HERE? The broken layer is the one where the answer changes between a working client and a failing one. Name it before you change anything.

tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.title: The request path as debuggable layers
tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.subtitle: Client → DNS → route → TLS → gateway → Service, each with the hook that interrogates it. Suspect edge: DNS resolves to a stale endpoint. The application handler is deliberately downstream and out of first scope.

tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.title: Running the path trace, one hook at a time
tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.subtitle: The inspection hooks that turn each layer from a guess into a verdict — the strong version of the artifact.
tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.code:
## 1. Path Trace — service.example.com fails for ~40% of clients
# L-DNS  does the name resolve to a LIVE endpoint?
dig +short service.example.com          # -> 10.0.4.9 (old pod, terminated)
# L-ROUTE does traffic reach the host at all?
traceroute -n 10.0.4.9                  # -> dies at last hop (no such target)
# L-TLS  is the certificate trusted for THIS name?
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 -servername service.example.com </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E 'Verify|CN='
# L-HTTP what does the app actually answer once connected?
curl -v https://service.example.com/health   # -> never reaches app: connect timeout
# L-POLICY is a NetworkPolicy silently dropping the pod?
kubectl describe networkpolicy -n orders | grep -A2 'Ingress'

- Suspect layer: DNS — stale A record points at a terminated endpoint
- Blast radius: ~40% of clients (those with the cached answer); no data loss
- Boundary: application handler NOT in scope until the path resolves clean

steps.label: DNS — the cheapest disqualifier
steps.note: dig +short is seconds and interrogates the very first layer. A stale A record record explains 'works for some' instantly: clients holding the old cached answer route to a dead IP.

steps.label: Route — did it even arrive?
steps.note: traceroute separates 'the packet never reached the host' from 'the host refused it'. A route that dies mid-path is a network cause, never an app bug.

steps.label: TLS — trusted for THIS name?
steps.note: openssl s_client with -servername checks SNI + cert validity. A cert valid for the old name but not the new one is the classic silent TLS break after a rename.

steps.label: HTTP — what the app actually says
steps.note: curl -v is the first hook that reaches HTTP semantics. If connect times out here, every layer ABOVE the app is still suspect — you have not reached the handler yet.

steps.label: Policy — the invisible deny
steps.note: kubectl describe networkpolicy surfaces a rule that drops traffic before the pod ever sees it. A policy deny looks exactly like an app hang from the client side.

steps.label: The verdict + boundary
steps.note: Name the suspect layer, the blast radius (stale ≠ lost), and what stays out of scope. The app handler is off-limits until the path is proven clean.

tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.caption: A reviewer replays dig +short, sees the stale IP, and confirms the cause before anyone opens the request handler.

tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.title: Debug the app vs trace the path
tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.subtitle: Same incident: 'service.example.com fails for ~40% of clients after a deploy.' Both feel like work; only one finds the cause.

left.label: Debug the application
lines: Re-read the request handler line by line
Add logging to the endpoint, redeploy
Blame the last code change ('must be mine')
No layer named — symptom treated as app bug
Never runs dig, openssl, or kubectl
left.verdict: Burns hours proving the code is innocent

right.label: Trace the TCP/IP path
lines: Walk DNS → route → TLS → HTTP → policy in order
One hook per layer, each able to return 'no'
dig +short exposes the stale A record in seconds
Suspect layer named; blast radius = cached clients
App handler explicitly out of scope until path is clean
right.verdict: Isolates the broken layer before opening a file

tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.caption: The 'works for some' split is a network signature. Debugging the app first is searching the one layer the evidence already cleared.

tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.text: The senior tell: they name the LAYER before the cause. 'It's DNS' is worth more than a hundred lines of handler logging, because it says which of five inspection hooks to run next. An engineer who can place a symptom on the right layer of the stack has already done 80% of the diagnosis — the command just confirms it.

tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.question: A service is reachable from some clients but times out for others, right after a deploy. Which move proves the cause fastest — and is a real kill-test?
options: Re-read the application handler, since it changed in the deploy.
Run dig +short against the name from a failing client and check whether it resolves to a live endpoint — a check whose answer eliminates or confirms the DNS layer.
Redeploy the service and see if the problem goes away.
Add more logging to the endpoint so you have something to show.
tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.explanation: The 'works for some' pattern points at the path, not the handler. dig +short interrogates the first and cheapest layer and can return 'no' (resolves to a live IP → DNS cleared) or 'yes' (stale/dead IP → cause found). Re-reading code (1) debugs the layer the evidence cleared; redeploy (3) and more logging (4) buy no information about which layer is broken.

tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.intro: Prove your Path Trace holds — no vibes:
items: Every symptom in your trace is placed on a specific layer (DNS, route, TLS, HTTP/proxy, or NetworkPolicy) — not left as 'the service is broken'.

Your suspect layer has at least one inspection hook attached (dig, traceroute, curl -v, openssl s_client, or kubectl describe networkpolicy) whose output would KILL the hypothesis if it came back clean.
You can explain why the 'works for some clients' split points at the path rather than the application handler.
The blast radius distinguishes severity — stale vs lost, degraded vs down — and names roughly who is affected.
The application handler is explicitly marked out of scope until the path resolves clean — and you can defend that boundary.

prompts: In your own words: why does 'reachable for some clients, dead for others' point at the network path instead of the application code?
Walk your five layers out loud — DNS, route, TLS, HTTP, policy — and name the one inspection hook that interrogates each.

tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.text: Trace-the-layer-before-you-fix travels to every layered system with a hidden cause. A regulated enterprise adds an mTLS layer and an egress firewall to the same path — same trace, two more hooks (openssl for client certs, a firewall rule review) before touching the app. A high-scale product spreads the DNS layer across GeoDNS and multiple load balancers, so 'works for some' becomes 'works in some regions' — but the move is identical: name the layer, run the hook, eliminate or confirm. Carry your network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md into the capstone: it is not 'I understand TCP/IP' but 'here is an incident I traced layer by layer, named the broken edge, and proved it with dig, openssl, and kubectl — read it.'

packet-path-reasoning.outcome: Take one real 'works for some clients, fails for others' incident (or a realistic one) and trace the packet path — DNS → route → TLS → HTTP/proxy → policy — to name the layer that actually fails, before you touch application code. Write it up as a decision packet with the constraint, the rejected explanation, the failure trigger, and the exact command output that proves the cause.
packet-path-reasoning.proof: network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md: a per-layer trace (DNS, route, TLS, HTTP/proxy, NetworkPolicy), the suspect layer marked, at least two inspection-hook outputs (dig / curl -v / openssl s_client / kubectl describe networkpolicy), the rejected 'it's the app code' explanation, and the invalidation condition. A reviewer can replay one command and land on the same layer you did.
packet-path-reasoning.unlock: Your packet reads as a directed path with the failing hop isolated by command evidence — not a guess about which service is 'probably' broken.
packet-path-reasoning.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'traced the packet path' if your evidence is application logs and a redeploy. Application symptoms are not a network cause. Until a dig / curl -v / openssl / policy check pins the hop, you have a hunch wearing a trace's clothes.

packet-path-reasoning.text: It works from your laptop and fails for half of production. The channel fills with app-code theories while the real fault is a stale DNS answer, an untrusted cert, an asymmetric route, or a NetworkPolicy that silently drops the packet — three hops before your code ever runs.

In Network Mental Models you learned the layers exist; packet path reasoning is the move that makes them pay off. It converts 'the service is flaky' into one directed path with a single failing hop you can point a command at — the trace that anchors every incident in this course.

packet-path-reasoning.prompt: A service is reachable from some clients and dead for others after a routine deploy. Your first instinct is to read the service's own logs. Good instinct — or a trap? Answer before reading on.
packet-path-reasoning.reveal: A trap. 'Reachable for some, dead for others' is the fingerprint of a NETWORK cause — DNS returning different answers per resolver, a cert some clients won't trust, route asymmetry, or a policy that only allows some source ranges. The service's own logs show it happily serving whoever reaches it, which quietly convinces you the code is fine and burns an hour. The packet often dies before it arrives — so trace the path first, read app logs last.

packet-path-reasoning.title: Trace the path before you change the system
packet-path-reasoning.text: Walk one request hop by hop — DNS lookup, IP route, TLS trust, HTTP/proxy semantics, firewall + NetworkPolicy — and find the first hop that fails. Separate what you can directly observe from what you infer. The failing hop, not the loudest service, is the cause.

packet-path-reasoning.title: The packet path — and where it dies
packet-path-reasoning.subtitle: One request, five decision points. The suspect hop (TLS trust) fails a subset of clients; the app never sees the request. DNS, route, and policy are the other places the packet can die before your code runs.

legend.label: app: sees only requests that survived the path

packet-path-reasoning.title: Tracing the path with four inspection hooks
packet-path-reasoning.subtitle: The exact commands from the decision packet — each one kills or confirms one hop. Run them in path order, top to bottom.
packet-path-reasoning.code:
# Hop 1 — DNS: does the name resolve, and to the SAME IP everywhere?
dig +short service.example.com            # us: 10.0.42.7   |  failing region: NXDOMAIN

# Hop 2/3 — route + TLS: can we connect, and is the cert chain trusted?
curl -v https://service.example.com/health
#   * Connected to service.example.com (10.0.42.7) port 443   <- route OK
#   * SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer cert  <- TLS FAILS here

# Confirm the TLS verdict directly (independent of curl's trust store)
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 -servername service.example.com </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E 'Verify|subject='
#   Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify the first certificate)   <- missing intermediate

# Hop 5 — policy: rule out a silent drop as an alternative cause
kubectl describe networkpolicy allow-frontend -n web | grep -A3 Ingress
#   From: podSelector app=frontend  (source range is allowed — not the cause here)

steps.label: Hop 1 — DNS first, always
steps.note: dig +short from a passing AND a failing vantage. Different answers (or NXDOMAIN for one region) means the packet never even aims at the right IP — stop here.

steps.label: Hops 2–3 — route then TLS in one shot
steps.note: curl -v prints 'Connected to <IP>' (route survived) then the TLS verdict. 'unable to get local issuer certificate' is a trust failure, not an app failure — the request dies mid-handshake.

steps.label: Confirm TLS independently
steps.note: openssl s_client bypasses curl's trust store. 'Verify return code: 21' pins it: the server isn't sending its intermediate cert, so clients without it cached reject the chain — exactly the 'some pass, some fail' split.

steps.label: Hop 5 — rule policy IN or OUT
steps.note: A NetworkPolicy that drops your source range produces the identical 'some clients fail' symptom. Checking it turns 'probably TLS' into 'TLS, and NOT a silent policy drop.'

packet-path-reasoning.caption: Two hooks confirm the cause (curl + openssl → cert chain), one rules out the look-alike (policy). That's decision proof + operational proof in four commands.

packet-path-reasoning.text: The senior tell in networking: 'reachable for some, broken for others' is almost never the application. It is per-resolver DNS, a cert chain missing its intermediate, route/NAT asymmetry, or a NetworkPolicy scoped to a subset of sources. A staff engineer distrusts symmetric app theories the moment the failure is asymmetric across clients — because the packet path, not the code, is where clients diverge.

packet-path-reasoning.question: A reviewer challenges your incident packet: 'You say it's a TLS trust issue — prove it's the network and not our code.' Which evidence actually settles it?
options: The service's own logs show no errors, so the code must be fine.

openssl s_client returns 'Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify the first certificate)' from a failing client and a clean handshake from a passing one — the request dies in the handshake, before any HTTP reaches the app.
You redeployed the service and it felt more stable afterward.
A teammate agrees it's 'probably a cert thing.'
packet-path-reasoning.explanation: Only option 2 is executable and layer-specific: the handshake fails on failing clients and succeeds on passing ones, so the packet dies at the TLS hop before HTTP — the app literally never receives the request. Quiet app logs (1) are consistent with a request that never arrived; a redeploy (3) and a teammate's vibe (4) prove nothing and can't be replayed by the reviewer.

curl -v + openssl pin the failing handshake
Passing vs failing client compared side by side
Rejected: 'app 502s' — app never got the request
Invalidation: 'if failing clients ALSO fail openssl, not TLS'

packet-path-reasoning.caption: Separate observed from inferred: 'Verify return code: 21' is observed; 'the app is broken' was inferred and wrong. The gold trace survives the reviewer because every hop verdict has a command behind it.

packet-path-reasoning.intro: Prove your packet path holds — no vibes:
items: You ran the trace in PATH ORDER (DNS → route → TLS → HTTP/proxy → policy), not in the order you assumed the bug lived. A skipped early hop can invalidate every later verdict.
At least two inspection hooks produced real output (dig, curl -v, openssl s_client, or kubectl describe networkpolicy) — and each output kills or confirms exactly one hop.
You compared a PASSING client to a FAILING one. 'Some pass, some fail' is only explained when you can show where the two paths diverge.
The rejected explanation ('it's the app code') is written down with the evidence that ruled it out — not silently dropped.
You wrote the invalidation condition: the observation that would prove your named hop is NOT the cause. If nothing could disprove it, you described the network instead of tracing it.

prompts: Walk your packet path out loud, hop by hop, naming the command that gave each hop its verdict — and which hop failed first.
Explain why 'reachable for some clients, failing for others' points at the network path before the application, using DNS or TLS from your own trace as the example.
Which explanation did you reject, and what exact output ('Verify return code: 21', an NXDOMAIN, a policy that didn't match) let you rule it out?

packet-path-reasoning.text: Trace-before-you-change is the whole game, and it scales by environment. On a small team the path is short — one DNS name, one cert, one host — and curl -v usually ends the investigation. In a regulated enterprise the same trace grows a NAT hop, a corporate proxy that re-terminates TLS, and split-horizon DNS, so 'some clients fail' hides in whose route crosses the proxy. At high scale, add QUIC, multiple CIDR ranges, load balancers with per-pod NetworkPolicy, and packet capture as the court of last resort. What stays invariant everywhere: name the failing hop with evidence before you touch the system. Carry network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md into the capstone — it is reused there as the incident trace, and a lesson whose artifact can't be replayed in the capstone isn't done.

latency-and-throughput.outcome: Take a real 'the service feels slow' complaint and separate latency (per-request delay) from throughput (requests/sec the path sustains). Write the Latency vs Throughput section of network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md: the measured symptom, which axis is actually bounded, the kill-test that proves it, and the fix you would REJECT because it targets the wrong axis.
latency-and-throughput.proof: Section of network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md that names the bounded axis (latency OR throughput), one dig/curl/openssl measurement that distinguishes them, a rejected fix with the reason it targets the wrong axis, and a reviewer objection. A peer reads it and can say which number they'd watch to know the fix worked.
latency-and-throughput.unlock: Your packet names the bounded axis, proves it with a measurement, and rejects a fix that would improve the OTHER axis.
latency-and-throughput.doNotClaim: Do not claim the service is 'slow' and stop there. 'Slow' is not a diagnosis — it hides whether each request is slow (latency) or too few fit through the pipe (throughput). Naming 'add more replicas' before you know which axis is bounded is a fix wearing a diagnosis's clothes.

latency-and-throughput.text: The dashboard is green on CPU, green on error rate, and the VP wants '/health made fast by Friday.' Three engineers are already sizing up a bigger load balancer — nobody has yet asked whether one request is slow or whether too many requests are queued behind each other. Those are two different bugs with two opposite fixes.

Latency is how long ONE request takes end to end; throughput is how many requests the path completes per second. They trade off and they fail differently — and confusing them is the classic networking miss where the team scales the wrong thing while the real bound sits in DNS, a TLS handshake, or a saturated link. This is the mental model the rest of the module debugs on top of.

latency-and-throughput.prompt: curl reports 40ms for a single /health call, yet under load p99 climbs to 4s. Is the service 'slow'? Which axis is actually bounded — and why does the single-shot 40ms almost prove the answer? Decide before reading.
latency-and-throughput.reveal: It is a throughput bound, not a latency bound. A lone request is fast (40ms), so the per-hop delay is fine — the 4s under load is queuing: requests arriving faster than the path drains, waiting in line. That is Little's Law in the wild (L = λ × W): raise arrival rate λ against a fixed service capacity and the queue length L — and therefore wait W — explodes, even though each request's own work never changed. 'Add a CDN to cut latency' would do nothing; you needed more concurrency or a faster service, not a shorter path.

latency-and-throughput.title: Latency is per-request delay; throughput is completions per second
latency-and-throughput.text: Latency = time for ONE request across the path (DNS + TLS + RTT + service). Throughput = requests/sec the path sustains. Under load, queuing turns a throughput bound into apparent latency. Measure a single request AND a saturated one — the gap tells you which axis is bounded.

latency-and-throughput.title: The request path — where latency accrues and where throughput is capped
latency-and-throughput.subtitle: One request pays latency at every hop (DNS → TLS → gateway → service → DB). Throughput is capped at the narrowest stage: here the connection pool. The queue in front of it is where a throughput bound masquerades as latency.

legend.label: throughput cap — queue forms here under load
service time (the axis a bigger box actually helps)

latency-and-throughput.title: The kill-test that separates the two axes
latency-and-throughput.subtitle: One curl for cold single-request latency, a hey/ab burst for saturated throughput. The gap between them IS the diagnosis.
latency-and-throughput.code:
# 1. LATENCY: one request, cold path, timing broken out per phase
curl -w 'dns:%{time_namelookup} tls:%{time_appconnect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer} total:%{time_total}\n' \
  -o /dev/null -s https://service.example.com/health
# -> dns:0.031 tls:0.088 ttfb:0.040 total:0.129   (one request is FAST)

# 2. THROUGHPUT: saturate the path, watch p99 and req/s
hey -z 30s -c 200 https://service.example.com/health
# -> Requests/sec: 512   p99 latency: 3.98s   (throughput floor + queuing blowup)

# 3. DISQUALIFY the latency story: is any single hop slow?
dig service.example.com +stats            # resolver RTT sane? (rules out DNS latency)
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 -servername service.example.com </dev/null
# handshake completes in one round -> TLS is not the per-request cost

# VERDICT: single=129ms, saturated p99=3.98s at 512 req/s
# -> bounded on THROUGHPUT (queuing), NOT per-request latency

steps.label: Measure one request's latency, per phase
steps.note: curl -w breaks total into DNS, TLS (appconnect), and TTFB. If total is small, no single hop is the per-request villain — latency is fine.

steps.label: Saturate to expose the throughput ceiling
steps.note: hey -c 200 drives concurrency. Requests/sec is the real throughput; the p99 blow-up is queuing, not slower work — each request still does 129ms of actual work.

steps.label: Rule out latency hops explicitly
steps.note: dig confirms resolver RTT is sane; openssl confirms the handshake is one round-trip, not a renegotiation. Both are the 'kill-tests' that eliminate the latency branch.

steps.label: Write the verdict as a gap
steps.note: 129ms single vs 3.98s saturated is a ~30x gap from concurrency alone. That gap is the signature of a throughput bound. Record the two numbers — they are the evidence a reviewer replays.

latency-and-throughput.caption: The move is two measurements, not one: a lone request AND a saturated path. One number can never tell latency from throughput; the gap between them can.

latency-and-throughput.title: Two diagnoses of the same 'it's slow' ticket
latency-and-throughput.subtitle: Symptom: p99 = 4s under load, single request = 129ms. Only one names the bounded axis and its wrong-axis fix.

left.label: Latency guess (wrong axis)
lines: Diagnosis: 'the service is slow'
Evidence: one number (p99 4s), taken under load
Fix: add a CDN / move region closer to cut RTT
Never measured a single cold request (129ms)
CDN caches nothing dynamic — p99 stays 4s
left.verdict: Targets latency; the bound was throughput — no change

right.label: Axis-separated diagnosis (gold)
lines: Single request 129ms (fast) vs saturated p99 3.98s
dig + openssl rule out DNS/TLS latency hops
Bounded axis: throughput — queue at the pool (size 512 req/s)
Fix: raise pool/concurrency or cut service time; not a CDN
Rejected: CDN — improves the non-bounded axis
right.verdict: Names the axis, proves it, rejects the wrong-axis fix

latency-and-throughput.caption: A CDN and a bigger connection pool solve DIFFERENT bugs. Naming the axis first is what stops you shipping the fix that changes nothing.

latency-and-throughput.text: The senior tell is knowing tail latency and throughput are governed together by queuing theory: as you push utilization toward 100% of a resource's throughput, wait time doesn't rise linearly — it goes vertical (the M/M/1 knee). That is why a service humming at 'only 85% CPU' can have a screaming p99. The number that predicts your 2 a.m. page is headroom-to-saturation, not average latency.

latency-and-throughput.question: A single curl to /orders returns in 90ms, but at 300 concurrent users p99 is 6s and DNS/TLS both measure clean. Which is the bounded axis and the correct class of fix?
options: Latency — put the service behind a CDN and use a closer region to cut round-trip time.
Throughput — the fast single request plus clean DNS/TLS point to queuing at a capacity ceiling; raise concurrency/pool size or reduce per-request service time.
Latency — the 6s p99 is the true per-request cost, so optimize the code path on the hot request.
Neither — 6s p99 under load is normal and needs no action.
latency-and-throughput.explanation: The lone request is fast (90ms) and DNS/TLS are clean, so no per-request hop is the villain — the 6s only appears under concurrency, which is the signature of queuing behind a throughput cap. The fix class is capacity/concurrency (more slots or less service time per request), not a CDN or region move (option 1), which target latency the diagnosis just ruled out.

latency-and-throughput.intro: Prove your axis call — no vibes:
items: You have TWO measurements recorded: a single cold request (curl -w with per-phase timing) and a saturated run (hey/ab with req/s + p99). One number alone cannot separate the axes.
The latency hops are explicitly ruled in or out: dig shows resolver RTT, openssl shows a one-round-trip handshake. If either is slow, latency is (also) bounded — say so.
The bounded axis is named in one word (latency OR throughput) and the gap between your two numbers supports it.
You wrote a REJECTED fix that targets the other axis, and one sentence on why it changes nothing (e.g. 'CDN caches no dynamic response').
A reviewer can point to the exact number they would watch on the dashboard to know the fix worked (p99 under load, or req/s at saturation) — not 'it should feel faster'.

prompts: In your own words: why can a service be low-latency and low-throughput at the same time — and how does queuing make a throughput bound LOOK like a latency problem?
Explain Little's Law (L = λ × W) using your own two measurements: what happens to wait W when arrival rate λ rises against fixed capacity?
State the wrong-axis fix you rejected and the one dashboard number that would have exposed it as useless.

latency-and-throughput.text: This axis-splitting is the whole game beyond networking. A checkout line: latency is how long the cashier takes per customer; throughput is customers/minute across all lanes — and a fast cashier with one lane still backs up at rush hour. A disk (IOPS vs seek time), an ML inference server (per-token latency vs tokens/sec), a highway (a car's trip time vs cars/hour) all fail the same two ways, and 'it's slow' hides which. You carry the same network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md into the next lesson, where this latency-vs-throughput split becomes the base for reading route asymmetry and policy drops — because you can't trace a slow path until you know whether it's slow per hop or slow under load.

failure-domain-mapping.text: It works from your laptop, it works from staging, and it is down for 30% of production — the same binary, the same request, a different answer depending on WHERE the client sits. The room is already three commits deep into the application code, and the real fault is one CIDR the new NetworkPolicy forgot to allow.

A request is not one hop — it is a chain: DNS resolve, IP route, TLS trust, HTTP semantics, load balancer, firewall, Kubernetes NetworkPolicy. Failure-domain mapping is the move that asks 'which link is actually broken?' before anyone touches code — the release/review-risk section of the incident packet you carry through this module.

failure-domain-mapping.prompt: A service is up for some clients and returns errors for others after a deploy. Your instinct says 'check the application logs first.' Is that the fastest path to the cause? Decide before reading on.
failure-domain-mapping.reveal: Usually no — it is searching where the light is good. 'Works for some clients, not others' is the signature of a DOMAIN split, not a code bug: split-horizon DNS returning different IPs, a certificate whose SAN is trusted by one client store and not another, an asymmetric route where the reply path is dropped, or a NetworkPolicy that allows one CIDR and denies another. The same request hitting the same code gets two answers only when something BELOW the code differs by client. Read the app logs and you will find a symptom; trace the path and you will find the cause.

failure-domain-mapping.title: The inspection hooks that pin the domain
failure-domain-mapping.subtitle: Four commands, walking DOWN the stack — each one clears a layer or convicts it. This is the evidence block of network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md.
failure-domain-mapping.code:
# 1. DNS — does every client resolve the SAME address?
dig +short service.example.com          # A: 10.0.4.12   B: 10.0.4.12  -> DNS cleared

# 2. TLS — is the served cert trusted and does the SAN match?
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 -servername service.example.com </dev/null 2>&1 \
  | grep -E 'subject=|Verify return code'
#   subject=CN=service.example.com   Verify return code: 0 (ok)  -> TLS cleared

# 3. HTTP — verbose, to see WHERE it stalls (connect? handshake? response?)
curl -v --max-time 5 https://service.example.com/health
#   * Connected to 10.0.4.12 ... then hangs, no response  -> stalls AFTER connect, BELOW HTTP

# 4. Kubernetes NetworkPolicy — the suspect: does an ingress rule cover client B's CIDR?
kubectl describe networkpolicy allow-clients -n orders
#   Allowing ingress from: 10.0.4.0/24   (client B is 10.0.9.0/24)  -> CONVICTED: policy drops B

steps.label: Clear DNS first (cheapest disqualifier)
steps.note: If A and B resolve to different IPs, the domain is split-horizon DNS and you stop here. Same IP for both → DNS is cleared, move down. Observed, not inferred.

steps.label: Clear TLS trust
steps.note: 'Verify return code: 0' with a matching SAN clears certificate trust. A code 21/verify failure that differs by client store is your domain — do not go deeper.

steps.label: curl -v localizes the stall
steps.note: Verbose curl shows the exact phase. 'Connected ... then hangs' means the TCP path is fine but nothing comes back — the drop is above connect and below HTTP: a policy or firewall silently discarding packets.

steps.label: Convict the NetworkPolicy
steps.note: The ingress rule allows 10.0.4.0/24; client B lives in 10.0.9.0/24. That single CIDR gap is the failure domain — packets from B are dropped before the Pod. This line IS the proof.

steps.label: Repair + re-run
steps.note: Add 10.0.9.0/24 to the ingress rule, then re-run curl -v from B. A response on the same hook is the before/after evidence the reviewer replays.

failure-domain-mapping.caption: Walk DOWN the stack, clearing each layer with an executable hook. The convicting line is the domain; the re-run after repair is the proof.

failure-domain-mapping.text: The senior tell: separate what you OBSERVED from what you INFERRED, and write down what would INVALIDATE your answer. And a finding that survives review states its own kill-switch — e.g. 'if B still fails after allowing 10.0.9.0/24, the domain is route asymmetry, not policy.' failure-domain-mapping.text: The same discipline hardens under stricter constraints. On a small team the packet is three hooks in a Slack thread; in a regulated enterprise the same trace must cite the firewall change ticket and the packet capture, and the repair goes through change control; at high scale the split-by-client symptom is often a single unhealthy load-balancer target or one AZ's route table, and the hooks run per-region. What stays invariant is the move: name the domain, clear the layers above it with executable evidence, convict one edge, repair, and re-run. What changes is the rigor of the proof and who has to sign it. This packet is the reusable core your capstone incident runbook is built on — not 'I understand networking,' but 'here is an outage I traced, convicted, repaired, and proved.'

dns-resolution.outcome: Take a real 'reachable for some clients, broken for others' scenario and turn DNS resolution into an INSPECTABLE decision: trace name resolution end-to-end, prove where the answer diverges, and write the network-path decision packet that separates a name-resolution cause from an application symptom.

A reviewer can replay your dig against the same name and land on the same authoritative answer.

dns-resolution.text: The service is up. Half the fleet reaches service.example.com fine; the other half gets connection refused after last night's cutover. Three engineers are already deep in the application logs — and the real fork happened three hops earlier, when two client resolvers returned two different A records for the same name.

This lesson opens the DNS / HTTP / TLS / QUIC module because name resolution is the first hop of every request — the answer chosen here decides which IP, which route, and which certificate everything downstream trusts. The recurring failure it kills: the team debugs application code while the real cause is that different clients are resolving the name to different answers.

dns-resolution.prompt: A service is reachable from some clients and refused by others. curl fails on the broken clients. Where do you look FIRST — the application, the load balancer, or somewhere earlier? Answer before reading on.
dns-resolution.reveal: Earlier. Before a single byte of HTTP is sent, the client must turn the name into an IP — and 'reachable for some, not others' is the signature of a resolution split: stale cache, a resolver pointing at a different view (split-horizon), a TTL that hasn't expired on half the fleet, or an NXDOMAIN on a stub resolver. Run `dig service.example.com` from a WORKING client and a BROKEN client. If the A records differ, you have found the fork before you have opened a single line of application code.

dns-resolution.title: DNS resolution is the answer every later hop trusts — prove it before the app
dns-resolution.text: Resolution walks stub → recursive resolver → root → TLD → authoritative, returning an A/AAAA record bounded by a TTL. The invariant: same name can yield different answers per resolver, cache, or view. Prove which answer the FAILING client got before blaming the application.

dns-resolution.subtitle: A query walks stub → recursive → root → TLD → authoritative, then caches under a TTL. The suspect edge is the recursive resolver's cache: on the failing client it holds a stale record from before the cutover. Everything downstream trusts whatever this hop returns.

dns-resolution.title: Tracing the fork with the inspection hooks
dns-resolution.subtitle: Run the same name from a working and a failing client. The commands ARE the evidence in the packet.
dns-resolution.code:
# 1. What answer does the FAILING client actually get?
dig +noall +answer service.example.com
# service.example.com. 42 IN A 10.2.4.9      <- stale: old IP, TTL still counting down

# 2. What is the TRUTH, straight from the authoritative NS (bypass every cache)?
dig +norecurse @ns1.example.com service.example.com
# service.example.com. 300 IN A 10.2.9.30    <- cutover IP the working clients have

# 3. Confirm the symptom is downstream of the wrong IP, not the app
curl -v --resolve service.example.com:443:10.2.9.30 https://service.example.com/health
# * Connected to service.example.com (10.2.9.30) port 443 -> 200 OK

# 4. Rule out a TLS-trust red herring on the correct IP
openssl s_client -connect 10.2.9.30:443 -servername service.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -dates

steps.label: Read the failing client's answer
steps.note: dig against the resolver the broken client uses. The stale A record (10.2.4.9) with a live TTL is the fork — half the fleet still cached the pre-cutover IP.

steps.label: Get ground truth from authoritative
steps.note: +norecurse @ns1 bypasses every cache and asks the zone's source of truth directly. 10.2.9.30 is the correct post-cutover answer. Two different answers for one name = a resolution split, confirmed.

steps.label: Prove the app is innocent
steps.note: curl --resolve pins the correct IP, skipping DNS entirely. A 200 here proves the application and route are healthy — the ONLY variable was the resolved IP.

steps.label: Clear TLS as a confound
steps.note: openssl s_client checks the cert on the correct IP matches the SNI name and is in date — so you can rule out cert trust before writing 'DNS' in the packet.

dns-resolution.caption: A reviewer re-runs step 2 against ns1 and lands on 10.2.9.30 too. That reproducible authoritative answer is the anchor the whole decision stands on.

dns-resolution.text: Read the TTL, not just the A record. RFC 1035 makes TTL the contract: a record cached with TTL 3600 can serve a stale answer for up to an hour after you 'fixed' DNS. The senior move before any cutover is to lower the TTL first, wait one old-TTL interval, THEN change the record — so the fleet converges in minutes instead of an unpredictable hour of split-brain resolution.

In a regulated enterprise with split-horizon DNS, internal and external clients resolve the SAME name to different views by design — so your dig must be run from inside each zone, and 'two different answers' may be correct, not a bug. In a high-scale product behind GeoDNS or a global load balancer, the authoritative answer varies by region and edge PoP, so you pin the resolver per region before comparing. http-semantics.text: The checkout endpoint returns 200 for the office VPN and hangs for half of mobile users after last night's ingress change. Three engineers are reading the order handler line by line — while the real fault is a POST being silently retried through an asymmetric route, double-charging the ones who reconnect.

HTTP semantics is the contract that says what a method promises (safe? idempotent?), what a status class means, and what is safe to retry — and that contract is what breaks first when DNS, TLS, or routing shifts underneath a service. This is Section 3 of the same incident packet you carry through this module, sitting between TLS trust and the proxy/load-balancer behavior above it.

http-semantics.prompt: A client sends POST /orders, the connection drops before any response arrives, and the client library retries. Is that safe? Answer before reading on.
http-semantics.reveal: Only if the server made POST idempotent — and by default it did not. GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS are SAFE and idempotent; PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe; POST is neither. A dropped connection is ambiguous: the request may have committed on the server even though no response reached the client. Retrying a non-idempotent POST across a flaky or asymmetric route is how one checkout becomes two charges. The fix is an Idempotency-Key, not more logging in the handler.

http-semantics.title: Semantics = method safety + idempotency + status class + retry rule
http-semantics.text: HTTP defines what each method promises: safe (no state change), idempotent (same result if repeated), or neither. Status classes carry meaning: 5xx often means the network path, not your code. The retry rule follows from idempotency — never auto-retry a non-idempotent request across an unproven path.

http-semantics.title: Where HTTP semantics breaks on the request path
http-semantics.subtitle: A POST /orders traverses DNS → TLS → gateway → two backends behind a policy. The retry (dashed) is only safe if the method is idempotent; the return path is asymmetric, so the client sees a timeout while the write commits. Payments settlement is out of scope.

http-semantics.title: Proving cause with inspection hooks, not the handler
http-semantics.subtitle: The evidence trail in network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md — separate signal from noise before touching code.
http-semantics.code:
# 1. Name resolution — does the client even reach the right IP?
dig +short service.example.com
#   93.184.216.34   <- expected edge; a split-horizon answer would betray DNS drift

# 2. HTTP semantics on the wire — method, status class, and retry safety
curl -v -X POST https://service.example.com/orders \
     -H 'Idempotency-Key: 8f2c-...' -d '{"sku":"A1"}'
#   > POST /orders HTTP/2
#   < HTTP/2 503                 <- 5xx = path/upstream, NOT the order handler
#   < retry-after: 2

# 3. TLS trust for the clients that fail (SNI must match the cert)
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 -servername service.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -dates
#   subject=CN=service.example.com   notAfter=... <- valid == rule TLS out

# 4. Route/policy asymmetry — is the RESPONSE path blocked one way?
kubectl describe networkpolicy orders-egress
#   Egress: to app=payments only  <- return traffic to client CIDR dropped -> timeout

steps.label: Resolve before you route
steps.note: dig proves the client hits the intended edge. A split-horizon or stale record explains 'works for some clients' before you ever read code.

steps.label: Read the semantics on the wire
steps.note: curl -v shows the method AND the status class. A 5xx is the network/upstream talking, not your handler — and the Idempotency-Key is what makes the retry the response invites actually safe.

steps.label: Rule TLS in or out
steps.note: openssl checks the cert the FAILING clients see. A valid, matching cert with good dates eliminates a whole branch — a passing test is pure profit.

steps.label: Find the asymmetry
steps.note: The policy allows egress to payments only, so the response to the client is dropped. The client times out and retries a non-idempotent POST — the real cause, invisible from inside the handler.

http-semantics.caption: Two hooks minimum. Here dig+openssl pass (name + trust are fine), curl shows a 5xx, and the NetworkPolicy names the asymmetric route — cause proven at the network layer, not guessed in app code.

http-semantics.text: RFC 9110 is explicit: a client MUST NOT automatically retry a non-idempotent request unless it has a way to know the request semantics are actually idempotent. A dropped connection is not evidence the write failed — it is evidence the response was lost. Senior tell: when someone says '5xx, so fix the endpoint,' the senior asks 'which 5xx, on which route, for which clients?' — because 502/503/504 are almost always the path, not the handler.

http-semantics.question: A production POST /orders works from the office network but times out and double-charges half of mobile clients after an ingress change. The team is debugging the order handler. What proves the real cause fastest?

curl -v the endpoint from a failing client's path to read the status class, then kubectl describe networkpolicy to check for an asymmetric return route — while confirming the POST has no idempotency guard.
Increase the client's HTTP retry count so the request eventually succeeds.
Switch the endpoint from POST to GET so it becomes safe to retry.
http-semantics.explanation: The symptom (works for some clients, double-charges on retry) points at the path plus non-idempotent semantics, not the handler. Option 2 separates signal from noise: the status class tells you it is upstream/route, the NetworkPolicy exposes the asymmetric return route, and the missing idempotency guard explains the double charge. More logging (1) and more retries (3) amplify the double-charge; turning an order write into a GET (4) breaks the semantics entirely — GET must be safe.

http-semantics.text: The move is domain-independent: name the contract, find where a change underneath it broke the contract, prove it with a cheap inspection before you touch code. In a stricter environment it tightens — a regulated payments API cannot rely on 'probably didn't commit', so idempotency keys and exactly-once semantics become mandatory, not optional; at high scale, a load balancer's own retry budget can amplify a non-idempotent request into a thundering herd. Same reasoning, higher stakes. Next lesson keeps this incident packet and moves up the stack to QUIC — where the transport changes but the semantic question 'is this safe to retry across a path I have not proven?' stays exactly the same.

tls-handshake-and-certificates.outcome: Take a real (or realistic) 'works for some clients, fails for others after a TLS change' incident and write the TLS section of network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md: the constraint, the selected trust/handshake approach, the rejected one, the exact failure trigger, and an openssl/curl verification trail another reviewer can replay.
tls-handshake-and-certificates.proof: The TLS section of network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md plus a tls_handshake_risk_register.md: a named constraint, chosen approach vs rejected option, a reproducible failure trigger, and at least one inspection-hook output (openssl s_client, curl -v, or a chain dump). A reviewer can point to the certificate/route evidence and replay the failure, not just read a description.
tls-handshake-and-certificates.unlock: Your packet names the operating constraint before the fix, records the rejected option, attaches one inspection-hook output, and states what would make the decision invalid.
tls-handshake-and-certificates.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'debugged the TLS issue' if your evidence is a green padlock in one browser. One client succeeding is exactly the trap: the failure lives on the clients that see a different SNI route, an incomplete chain, or an untrusted root. Proof is an openssl handshake that fails the same way the customer's does — not the one that works on your laptop.

tls-handshake-and-certificates.text: The status page is green, the padlock shows in your browser, and the pager keeps firing: half the customers get 'certificate not trusted' and the other half never notice. Someone is already rewriting the application error handler — while the real fault is a missing intermediate certificate the server never sends.

This lesson sits inside DNS · HTTP · TLS · QUIC, right after name resolution and HTTP semantics. A reachable-for-some, broken-for-others service is a networking problem, so completion means a decision artifact, a risk note, and an openssl/curl verification trail a reviewer can inspect.

tls-handshake-and-certificates.prompt: curl https://service.example.com/health returns 'unable to get local issuer certificate', but the site loads fine in your browser. Before you touch server code — what is the most likely cause? Decide first.
tls-handshake-and-certificates.reveal: The server is not sending its full certificate chain. Your browser silently patched the gap from a cached intermediate it fetched earlier (AIA fetching); curl and many API clients do not. The leaf is valid, the root is trusted — the missing link is the intermediate CA in between. 'It works in my browser' is the false-positive that hides an incomplete chain from every non-browser client on the network.

tls-handshake-and-certificates.title: TLS trust is a chain the server must present, not a single cert
tls-handshake-and-certificates.text: The handshake proves identity by presenting leaf + intermediate certificates that chain to a root the client already trusts, for the SNI hostname requested. Trust fails when any link is missing, expired, name-mismatched, or absent from the client's trust store — even when the leaf itself is valid.

tls-handshake-and-certificates.title: The TLS handshake and the chain that must validate
tls-handshake-and-certificates.subtitle: Client sends SNI in ClientHello; server returns the leaf + intermediate for that name; the client walks the chain to a trusted root. The missing-intermediate edge is where 'works for some' breaks.

legend.label: SNI decides which cert the server sends
root must already be trusted client-side

tls-handshake-and-certificates.title: The inspection hook that proves it: openssl s_client
tls-handshake-and-certificates.subtitle: One command separates 'my code' from 'the chain'. Read the verify line and the chain depth, not the app response.
tls-handshake-and-certificates.code:
# Probe the exact chain the server sends for this SNI hostname
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 \
  -servername service.example.com -showcerts </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl_chain_dump

# What a BROKEN (missing-intermediate) handshake shows:
#   Certificate chain
#    0 s:CN=service.example.com   i:CN=R3 Intermediate
#   verify error:num=20:unable to get local issuer certificate
#   Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify the first certificate)

# Compare against the client's real trust store, non-browser:
curl -v https://service.example.com/health 2>&1 | grep -Ei 'SSL|subject|issuer|verify'

# Confirm SNI routing: does a different name get a different cert?
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 \
  -servername OTHER-vhost.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | grep 'subject='

steps.label: Pin the SNI explicitly
steps.note: -servername forces the exact name the failing client sends. Skip this and you test a different virtual host than the customer hit — the whole point of 'works for some'.

steps.label: Dump every cert the server actually sends
steps.note: -showcerts is the evidence: it prints the chain on the wire, not what the CA issued you. A one-cert chain here is the missing intermediate, caught.

steps.label: Read the verify line, not the page
steps.note: 'unable to get local issuer certificate' + return code 21 is the smoking gun. This is network evidence — it names the cause before you open any application file.

steps.label: Reproduce with the client's real trust store
steps.note: curl uses the OS/CA bundle a browser bypasses. If curl fails where the browser passes, the chain is incomplete, not your code.

steps.label: Falsify the SNI-routing hypothesis
steps.note: A different -servername returning a different subject proves the load balancer selects certs by SNI — the 'some clients' asymmetry made visible.

tls-handshake-and-certificates.caption: verify return code 21 with a depth-0-only chain = server omits the intermediate. Repair is a server-side fullchain, not an app change — and this output is the before-half of the repair report.

tls-handshake-and-certificates.title: Two TLS incident write-ups, same outage
tls-handshake-and-certificates.subtitle: Service reachable for browsers, failing for API clients after a cert rotation. Both name TLS; only one is inspectable.

left.label: Described, not proven
lines: Constraint: none stated
Evidence: 'padlock is green in Chrome'
Cause: 'probably a cert issue'
Fix: bumped the app's error handling + retries
No SNI pinned, no chain dump, no client trust store checked
Rejected option + invalidation condition: absent
left.verdict: False confidence — debugs app code while the chain stays broken

right.label: Proven with inspection hooks
lines: Constraint: no daytime downtime; rotation must not break API clients
Evidence: openssl s_client -servername → verify code 21, depth-0-only chain
Cause: server presents leaf only; intermediate omitted post-rotation
Fix: deploy fullchain (leaf+intermediate); re-run probe → code 0
Rejected: pin new root client-side — too slow, misses third parties
Invalidation: any client whose trust store lacks the root still fails
right.verdict: Replayable — reviewer reruns the probe and sees code 21 → 0

tls-handshake-and-certificates.caption: The gold version separates network cause from application symptom: the openssl verify code is observable, the rejected option is recorded, and the invalidation condition names who still breaks.

tls-handshake-and-certificates.text: The senior tell in TLS incidents: never trust a browser as your test client. Browsers hide server misconfiguration with AIA intermediate-fetching, cached OCSP, and per-vendor root stores. Your API callers, mobile SDKs, and Kubernetes sidecars use a strict CA bundle and no fetching — so 'works in my browser, fails in curl' is not a fluke, it is the exact signature of an incomplete chain or a client-trust-store gap.

tls-handshake-and-certificates.question: A reviewer challenges: 'Prove this TLS failure is real and not just described.' Which evidence actually proves it?
options: A screenshot of the site loading with a padlock in your browser.
openssl s_client -servername <host> output showing the on-the-wire chain and 'Verify return code: 21', reproduced by curl against the client's CA bundle.
A note saying 'the certificate looks fine in the dashboard'.
The application logs showing 500 errors after the TLS layer.
tls-handshake-and-certificates.explanation: Only option 2 is network evidence a reviewer can replay: it pins the SNI, dumps the exact chain the server sends, and reads the TLS verify code against a real (non-browser) trust store. The padlock (1) is the false-positive this lesson exists to kill; the dashboard (3) is a description; app 500s (4) are the downstream symptom, not the certificate cause.

tls-handshake-and-certificates.intro: Prove the TLS decision holds — no padlocks, no vibes:
items: You pinned the failing client's SNI with -servername; you are testing the same virtual host the customer hit, not a default vhost.
You have the on-the-wire chain from -showcerts and can point to the exact missing/expired/mismatched link — not just 'a cert issue'.
You reproduced the failure with curl (or the real SDK) against the client's actual CA bundle, so a browser's silent fetching cannot mask it.
The packet records the rejected approach (e.g. client-side root pinning) and why it fails under the no-daytime-downtime constraint.
You wrote the invalidation condition: the client population whose trust store would still fail even after your fix.

prompts: In your own words: why does 'it works in my browser' actively mislead you when API clients are failing TLS?
Explain the difference between a valid leaf certificate and a valid chain, using your own openssl output as the example.
What was your rejected option, and which constraint (downtime? third-party clients?) eliminated it before you diagnosed anything?

tls-handshake-and-certificates.text: The same move — pin the exact identity requested, dump what the server actually presents, validate it against the consumer's real trust store — travels straight into the next layer. In Kubernetes, an Ingress terminating TLS with a partial chain fails the same way for pod-to-pod mTLS sidecars that use a strict CA bundle; the probe is openssl inside the pod instead of on your laptop. In a stricter regulated environment, add pinned roots and short-lived certs, and the invalidation condition grows: every rotation is now a potential 'works-for-some' incident. This TLS section is not a throwaway — it becomes the trust-and-identity layer of the capstone's network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md, sitting beside the DNS resolution and route-asymmetry findings so a reviewer can trace one request from name lookup through certificate trust to the stale-for-some response.

quic-tradeoffs.outcome: Take one real service you would move to HTTP/3 (or a realistic one) and write the QUIC decision: the operating constraint (who reaches it, over what path), the approach you'd choose, the approach you'd reject, and the exact failure QUIC introduces — then attach the inspection-hook output that proves it. Produce network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md.
quic-tradeoffs.proof: network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md with: context, assumptions, selected approach, rejected approach, the QUIC-specific failure (UDP/443 blocked → who is affected), verification method (dig/curl --http3/openssl), reviewer objection, and repair notes. A reviewer can replay the failure and see how a client falls back — not just read a claim that it 'works'.
quic-tradeoffs.unlock: Your packet names the constraint before the fix, records the rejected option and WHY it fails under release/review risk, and carries one real hook output (curl --http3-only failing, curl succeeding on h2).
quic-tradeoffs.doNotClaim: Do not claim 'QUIC is faster so we should adopt it.' Faster on the happy path is not the decision. If your packet has no failure trigger (a client behind a UDP-blocking firewall) and no fallback evidence, you described QUIC — you did not decide it.

quic-tradeoffs.text: You flip the service to HTTP/3 on Friday. Latency drops for most users — and then a corporate customer whose firewall silently drops UDP/443 can't reach you at all, while your dashboards stay green because they only measure the clients that connected.

QUIC rides UDP and folds TLS 1.3 into the handshake, so it buys you 0-RTT resumption and connection migration — but it also moves you off the TCP path every middlebox on Earth already trusts. This lesson lives in Module 2 because you've traced DNS, HTTP, and TLS separately; QUIC is where those layers collapse into one flight and the tradeoff becomes a release decision.

quic-tradeoffs.prompt: Your load test says QUIC cuts p50 connection time by 40%. Is that enough to ship HTTP/3 to all clients? Answer before reading on.
quic-tradeoffs.reveal: No — the load test only measured clients that completed a QUIC handshake. The population that matters most is the one your test can't see: users behind firewalls, NATs, or middleboxes that block or mangle UDP/443. QUIC's real design bet is the fallback: a browser races QUIC against TCP+TLS and quietly drops to HTTP/2 when UDP fails. Your 40% win is real for the reachable; the decision is about the unreachable, and 'faster' says nothing about them.

quic-tradeoffs.title: QUIC trades middlebox-trust for a faster, migratable handshake
quic-tradeoffs.text: QUIC = TLS 1.3 + streams over UDP/443: 1-RTT (0-RTT on resume), no head-of-line blocking, survives IP changes via connection ID. The cost: UDP is second-class on the internet, so reachability now depends on fallback to TCP+TLS.

quic-tradeoffs.title: Two clients, one origin — where QUIC wins and where it must fall back
quic-tradeoffs.subtitle: The happy path (UDP/443 open) gets 0-RTT and migration. The blocked path (firewall drops UDP) MUST fail over to TCP+TLS/HTTP2 or the customer sees an outage. The fallback edge is the whole decision.

legend.label: the fallback that saves the customer

quic-tradeoffs.title: The decision packet, proven with dig / curl / openssl
quic-tradeoffs.subtitle: network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md — a constraint, the rejected option, and the exact hooks that separate 'described' from 'proven'.
quic-tradeoffs.code:
# Network Path Debug & Incident Packet — HTTP/3 (QUIC) rollout
## Context
Move api.example.com from HTTP/2 (TCP/443) to HTTP/3 (QUIC, UDP/443).
Constraint: 12% of traffic is enterprise clients behind egress firewalls.
## Selected approach
Dual-stack: advertise h3 via Alt-Svc, KEEP TCP+TLS/HTTP2 listening.
## Rejected approach
UDP-only HTTP/3 (drop TCP). Rejected: any UDP-blocking middlebox = hard outage.
## Verify (inspection hooks)
dig +short api.example.com                 # A/AAAA resolve first — rule out DNS
curl -sI --http3-only https://api.example.com/health   # QUIC-only: expect FAIL from corp
curl -sI --http2      https://api.example.com/health   # fallback path: expect 200
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -tls1_3 -alpn h2  </dev/null | grep -E 'ALPN|Verify'
## Expected failure (the QUIC-specific one)
UDP/443 dropped silently by firewall -> handshake never completes ->
dashboards stay green (only measure connected clients) -> corp users dark.
## Reviewer objection
"Is HTTP/3 proven reachable, or only fast for clients that got through?"
## Repair notes
Keep Alt-Svc TTL short; alert on h3:h2 negotiation ratio drop, not just p50.

steps.label: Constraint before fix
steps.note: Name WHO is on the path (12% enterprise, egress firewalls) before naming HTTP/3. The constraint is what rules the rejected option out.

steps.label: The rejected option, with a reason
steps.note: UDP-only is the seductive answer — fewer sockets, pure QUIC. Rejected because one UDP-blocking middlebox turns a speed win into a hard outage for the client who complains loudest.

steps.label: Hook 1 — rule out DNS first
steps.note: dig confirms name resolution isn't the cause. Networking's #1 trap: debugging the app while the real issue is resolution, trust, or policy.

steps.label: Hooks 2+3 — force each path
steps.note: --http3-only proves the QUIC path FAILS from a blocked client (the failure trigger); --http2 proves the fallback SUCCEEDS. Two commands, one falsifiable decision.

steps.label: Hook 4 — confirm ALPN + trust on fallback
steps.note: openssl shows the TCP path negotiates h2 with a valid cert chain — the fallback isn't just reachable, it's TLS-sound.

steps.label: The invalidation condition
steps.note: Green dashboards that only measure connected clients are the false-confidence trap. The repair alerts on the h3:h2 ratio — a reachability signal, not a latency one.

quic-tradeoffs.caption: Two curls decide it: --http3-only fails from the corp client, --http2 returns 200. The fallback is the product; the speed is the bonus.

quic-tradeoffs.title: Two HTTP/3 rollout plans, same origin
quic-tradeoffs.subtitle: One optimizes the happy-path benchmark; one survives the client behind the firewall.

left.label: UDP-only, benchmark-driven
lines: Ship HTTP/3, drop TCP/443 to 'simplify'
Constraint (enterprise egress) never named
No fallback path — UDP is the only door
Proof = p50 load test on reachable clients
Firewall drops UDP → corp customer goes dark, silently
left.verdict: Fast in review, hard outage on release

right.label: Dual-stack, reachability-first
lines: Advertise h3 via Alt-Svc, KEEP TCP+TLS/HTTP2
Constraint stated: 12% behind UDP-blocking firewalls
Fallback proven: --http3-only fails, --http2 = 200
Alert on h3:h2 negotiation ratio, not just p50
Rejected option (UDP-only) recorded with its failure
right.verdict: Faster for most, reachable for all

quic-tradeoffs.caption: The gold plan is INSPECTABLE: a reviewer can replay the blocked path and watch the client fall back to HTTP/2. The weak plan can only be trusted, not tested.

quic-tradeoffs.text: The standards make the fallback mandatory, not optional: RFC 9114 (HTTP/3) is discovered via the Alt-Svc header (RFC 7838) layered over an existing HTTP/2 origin — the client only tries QUIC after it already has a TCP answer. That's why 'HTTP/3-only' fights the protocol's own design. The senior tell: you don't measure a QUIC rollout by p50, you measure it by the h3-vs-h2 negotiation ratio — the clients quietly on h2 are your reachability canary.

quic-tradeoffs.question: A reviewer asks: 'Prove your HTTP/3 rollout is reachable, not just fast.' Which evidence answers the challenge?
options: A load test showing QUIC cuts p50 connection time 40% for clients that connected.
curl --http3-only failing from a UDP-blocked client AND curl --http2 returning 200 for that same client, plus an alert on the h3:h2 negotiation ratio.
A statement that browsers 'handle fallback automatically,' so no test is needed.
openssl output proving the TLS 1.3 certificate chain is valid on UDP/443.
quic-tradeoffs.explanation: Reachability is proven by exercising the FAILURE path and the fallback: --http3-only must be able to fail (option 1 only measures the reachable, so it's blind to the population at risk), and --http2 must succeed for that same blocked client. The ratio alert makes silent degradation visible. 'Handled automatically' (3) is an unverified claim, and a valid cert on UDP/443 (4) says nothing about clients who can't reach UDP at all.

quic-tradeoffs.intro: Prove your QUIC decision holds — no vibes:
items: Run dig first. Confirm A/AAAA resolve, so you can rule DNS out before blaming QUIC — separate the network cause from the app symptom.
Run curl --http3-only against a UDP-blocked path. If it CANNOT fail, you have no failure trigger and cannot prove reachability — construct the blocked case.
Run curl --http2 for that same client and confirm a 200. The fallback must be demonstrably reachable, not assumed.
Check your packet names the rejected approach (UDP-only) AND why it fails under release/review risk — a decision with no rejected option is a preference.
Confirm your monitoring alerts on the h3:h2 negotiation ratio, not only p50 — otherwise green dashboards will hide the exact users QUIC broke.

prompts: In your own words: what does QUIC actually trade away to get 0-RTT and connection migration, and who pays that cost?
Explain why a p50 latency benchmark is the wrong proof for a QUIC rollout, using your own packet's failure trigger as the example.
Your reviewer says 'browsers fall back automatically, ship it.' Give the one-sentence reason that's true and still insufficient — and name the exact hook output that closes the gap.

quic-tradeoffs.text: The move isn't QUIC — it's 'the benchmark measures the reachable; the decision is about the unreachable.' Take it to a stricter environment and the invariant holds while the constraint changes: in a regulated enterprise, a deep-packet-inspection firewall may block QUIC by policy, so dual-stack isn't optimization, it's a compliance requirement; at high scale, UDP amplification and load-balancer connection-ID routing become the dominant cost, and the h3:h2 ratio becomes an SLO. Same reasoning — name the path, force the failure, prove the fallback. This packet is your capstone evidence: not 'I understand QUIC' but 'here is a rollout I framed, broke on a blocked client, and proved reachable — read it.'

cidr-and-subnets.outcome: Take one real network boundary you own (a VPC, a Kubernetes cluster, an office-to-cloud link) and write the CIDR Plan: the address space, a non-overlapping subnet split by function and AZ, the reserved/usable host math, and the one route or policy decision the split forces. Then produce cidr_and_subnets_decision_packet.md with a constraint table, chosen block, rejected block, and the verification you ran.
cidr-and-subnets.proof: cidr_and_subnets_decision_packet.md: a chosen VPC block (e.g. 10.20.0.0/16), a subnet table with prefix, first/last usable, host count, and AZ, zero overlap with any peered/on-prem range, one rejected sizing and why, plus a verification trail (ipcalc or a route/NetworkPolicy check) a reviewer can replay. A peer confirms no two subnets overlap and the block is big enough to grow.
cidr-and-subnets.unlock: Your plan names the address space, splits it without overlap, shows the usable-host math per subnet, and states the route/peering decision the split forces.
cidr-and-subnets.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'subnetted' if you only picked a /16 and eyeballed it. A plan without the actual first/last-usable boundaries and an overlap check against every peer is a guess. The math IS the artifact — a reviewer must be able to point at two ranges and confirm they cannot collide.

cidr-and-subnets.text: Two teams peer their VPCs on launch day and everything east-west goes dark — both quietly chose 10.0.0.0/16, so the router has two identical destinations and silently drops half the traffic. Nobody touched application code; the whole outage was an address-space decision made months earlier with no overlap check.

CIDR is how you carve a finite address space into non-overlapping, right-sized boundaries — the substrate every route, firewall rule, and peering connection is written against. Get the split wrong and the failure shows up later as asymmetric routing or a silent policy drop that looks like an app bug. This is Section 1 of a decision packet you carry through the routing and load-balancing module.

cidr-and-subnets.prompt: You need room for 500 hosts in a subnet. Someone reaches for a /24. Before you agree — what breaks, and what should the prefix be? Answer before reading on.
cidr-and-subnets.reveal: A /24 gives 256 addresses and only 254 usable — it cannot hold 500 hosts. Each subnet loses TWO addresses: the network address (all-zero host bits) and the broadcast address (all-one host bits). For 500 hosts you need a /23 (512 total, 510 usable). The trap is thinking a /24 means '256 usable' and that bigger numbers after the slash mean bigger networks — it is the reverse: a SMALLER prefix means MORE hosts. /23 is bigger than /24.

cidr-and-subnets.title: A prefix draws the line between network and host bits
cidr-and-subnets.text: CIDR /n fixes the first n bits as the network; the remaining 32−n are host bits. Usable hosts = 2^(32−n) − 2 (network + broadcast reserved). Smaller n means a bigger block. The invariant: subnets under one parent must not overlap.

cidr-and-subnets.title: Splitting 10.20.0.0/16 into a non-overlapping VPC plan
cidr-and-subnets.subtitle: One /16 parent carved into public, private-app, and data tiers across two AZs. Every child is disjoint; the peered on-prem /16 is out of scope and must never overlap. The suspect edge is the peering boundary where a duplicate range silently drops traffic.

cidr-and-subnets.title: Proving the split with ipcalc, one line at a time
cidr-and-subnets.subtitle: The real artifact: the exact boundaries and host counts a reviewer replays. Numbers are computed, not eyeballed.
cidr-and-subnets.code:
# CIDR Plan — VPC 10.20.0.0/16  (65,536 addresses total)
$ ipcalc 10.20.0.0/16
Network:   10.20.0.0/16
HostMin:   10.20.0.1    HostMax: 10.20.255.254   Hosts: 65534

# Public tier  — LBs + NAT gateways (one /20 spans both AZs)
#   10.20.0.0/20   -> HostMin 10.20.0.1   HostMax 10.20.15.254   (4094 usable)
# App tier AZ-a  10.20.16.0/20 -> 10.20.16.1  .. 10.20.31.254  (4094 usable)
# App tier AZ-b  10.20.32.0/20 -> 10.20.32.1  .. 10.20.47.254  (4094 usable)
# Data tier      10.20.48.0/22 -> 10.20.48.1  .. 10.20.51.254  (1022 usable)

# Overlap check vs peered on-prem 10.10.0.0/16 -> DISJOINT (10.20 != 10.10). PASS
# Rejected: single flat /24 per tier -> 254 hosts, too small for app fleet. REJECT

steps.label: Anchor the parent
steps.note: A /16 = 2^16 = 65,536 addresses, 65,534 usable. This is the budget every child spends from — you cannot allocate more than this.

steps.label: Public /20 carved from the top
steps.note: A /20 = 2^(32-20) = 4096 addresses, 4094 usable. HostMin is network+1, HostMax is broadcast−1. Spans both AZs on purpose — LBs are AZ-agnostic here.

steps.label: Two app /20s, one per AZ
steps.note: AZ-a starts at .16.0 and AZ-b at .32.0 — the next /20 boundary each time. Aligning on the boundary is what guarantees no overlap; an off-boundary start collides.

steps.label: Data tier sized tight
steps.note: A /22 = 1022 usable — plenty for a managed DB subnet group, and small on purpose so the blast radius of a data-tier rule is contained.

steps.label: The overlap check (the whole point)
steps.note: Second octet 20 vs 10 differ, so the two /16s are disjoint — no route ambiguity across the peering link. This is the line that would have prevented the launch-day outage.

steps.label: The rejected option, on the record
steps.note: A flat /24 per tier caps at 254 hosts. Naming why it fails under the growth constraint is what turns a pick into a decision.

cidr-and-subnets.caption: A reviewer replays ipcalc on any row and confirms the host range — and confirms 10.20.x never meets 10.10.x.

/24 for 500 hosts (only 254 usable)
No first/last-usable math written down
No overlap check against the peered range
Subnets not aligned on prefix boundaries

lines: Parent /16 carved into boundary-aligned /20s + /22
