service-discovery.caption: The weak version debugs the application while name resolution and policy — the real causes — go unexamined. Proof lives in hook output, not adjectives.

service-discovery.question: A reviewer challenges your packet: "Prove this is service discovery, not an app bug." What is the exact evidence that settles it?
options: The application logs show connection timeouts, so the network must be at fault.
Side-by-side dig / curl -v run from BOTH the failing and working pod, showing the name resolves (or the policy allows) differently between them.
You restarted the deployment and it worked for a while.
The service has an uptime SLA, so discovery should be reliable.
service-discovery.explanation: The failure is asymmetric — some clients work, some fail — and the application code is identical for both, so app logs (1) cannot discriminate cause from symptom. Only a diff of the SAME inspection hook from the failing vs working pod isolates the layer: different resolution, a policy that allows A but not B, or a cert trust error on one path. A restart (3) and an SLA (4) are not evidence.

service-discovery.intro: Prove the packet is inspectable — no vibes:
items: Every claim in the packet has a hook output beside it (dig, curl -v, openssl s_client, or kubectl describe networkpolicy) — a bare assertion with no command is not proof.
At least one hook was run from INSIDE the failing pod, not from a shell that already works.
You used at least two different hooks, spanning at least two layers (e.g. DNS and policy, or DNS and TLS).
The rejected explanation is recorded with why it fails — an explanation that only your favored cause survives is theater.
The invalidation condition is written: state the exact result that would force you to reopen the case at a different layer.

prompts: Trace the path out loud from the failing pod: name each hop (resolve → route → trust → HTTP) and the one command that proves it.
Explain why running dig from a working shell would have hidden this bug, using your own packet as the example.
Name the layer your cause lives on, the explanation you rejected, and the single result that would prove your whole packet wrong.

service-discovery.text: The same discipline scales up and down. On a smaller team the packet shrinks to two commands and a Slack thread; in a regulated enterprise it grows a change-control ID and a signed incident timeline; at high scale you add per-region diffs because "works in us-east, fails in eu-west" is the asymmetry writ large. What stays invariant: trace the path, prove each hop with a hook, name the layer, and state what would invalidate you. This packet is your capstone evidence — not "I understand service discovery" but "here is a discovery failure I traced, proved at the network layer, and repaired." Carry network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md into the capstone unchanged in structure.

ingress-and-services.outcome: Take a real (or realistic) 'reachable for some clients, broken for others' incident and write the network-path decision packet: name the operating constraint, trace the path layer by layer (DNS → route → TLS → HTTP → Service/Ingress → NetworkPolicy), pick a fix, name the rejected fix, and attach at least two inspection-hook outputs as proof.
ingress-and-services.proof: network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md with a constraint table, a layer-by-layer path trace, selected vs rejected approach, a failure trigger, and ≥2 real hook outputs (dig / curl -v / openssl s_client / kubectl describe networkpolicy). A reviewer can replay the failure and point to the exact line that proves name resolution, cert trust, route asymmetry, or policy — not app code — is the cause. Plus network_path_debug_and_incident_risk_register.md with the top 3 residual risks.
ingress-and-services.unlock: Your packet names the constraint before the fix, distinguishes application symptom from network cause, and carries observable proof at the failing layer.
ingress-and-services.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'debugged the ingress' if your only evidence is that a curl worked from your laptop. One client succeeding proves nothing about the client that fails — route asymmetry, split-horizon DNS, and per-namespace NetworkPolicy all pass from the happy path. Proof lives on the FAILING path, not the working one.

ingress-and-services.text: The service is green on every dashboard, half the customers can reach it, and three engineers are already rewriting the handler that 'must be dropping requests.' Nobody has run a single dig from the client that fails — so nobody yet knows the app was never the problem.

In Kubernetes a request crosses DNS, IP routing, TLS trust, HTTP semantics, the Service's kube-proxy hop, the Ingress router, and NetworkPolicy before it ever reaches your code. 'Works for some, fails for others' is the signature of a network-path fault — and this packet is where you prove which layer, with evidence a reviewer can replay.

ingress-and-services.prompt: A Service is reachable from pods in namespace A but times out from namespace B. Same image, same replicas, same Ingress. Where do you look first — the application, or somewhere else? Decide before reading on.
ingress-and-services.reveal: Not the application — identical code cannot behave differently by caller namespace. That asymmetry is the tell: a default-deny NetworkPolicy in namespace B (or a missing ingress rule allowing A but not B) is silently dropping the connection before HTTP begins. 'kubectl describe networkpolicy' in B settles it in seconds; re-reading the handler would burn the night. When the SAME service answers some callers and not others, the variable is the PATH, never the code.

ingress-and-services.title: Trace the path, layer by layer, before you touch the system
ingress-and-services.text: A request is DNS → route → TLS → HTTP → Service → Ingress → NetworkPolicy. Walk it in order, separate what you can observe from what you infer, and prove the failing layer. Asymmetry (some clients, not others) means the cause is on the path, not in the code.

ingress-and-services.title: The request path: where 'reachable for some, broken for others' hides
ingress-and-services.subtitle: External client → DNS → Ingress (TLS terminates) → Service (kube-proxy) → Pod. NetworkPolicy gates the Service edge; the internal client's request is silently dropped there — the app is never reached.

nodes.label: Pod
nodes.description: the app — never the cause here

legend.label: on the suspect path (TLS · route · Service)
the drop point — NetworkPolicy denies ns B
healthy: the app + the client that works

ingress-and-services.title: The decision packet: tracing the failing layer with real hooks
ingress-and-services.subtitle: network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md — each hook eliminates one layer until the drop is proven.
ingress-and-services.code:
## Constraint
# No daytime downtime on the checkout path; fix must not restart the Ingress.

## Layer trace (external client = OK, internal ns B = FAIL)
# L1 DNS  — resolves to the LB, so name resolution is NOT the fault:
dig +short api.example.com            # 203.0.113.10  (external)
dig +short api.example.com @10.96.0.10 # 10.100.4.7   (in-cluster ClusterIP)

# L3/L4 route + L6 TLS — external path is clean end to end:
curl -v https://api.example.com/health            # < HTTP/2 200
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com </dev/null 2>&1 | grep 'Verify return'
#   Verify return code: 0 (ok)   → cert chain trusted, TLS is NOT the fault

# L7 from the FAILING client — hangs, no HTTP response at all:
kubectl -n ns-b run probe --image=curlimages/curl --rm -it -- \
  curl -sS --max-time 5 http://api.svc.cluster.local/health   # timeout, exit 28

# Policy — the drop: ns B is absent from the ingress allow-list:
kubectl describe networkpolicy api-allow -n api-ns
#   Allowing ingress from: NamespaceSelector team=a   (ns B has team=b)

## Selected approach: add team=b to the NetworkPolicy from-selector (hot-apply, no restart)
## Rejected approach: loosen to Allow-All ingress — removes the isolation the constraint depends on
## Failure trigger: any client whose namespace label is not in the from-selector
## Verification: re-run the ns-b probe → expect HTTP 200; capture before/after

steps.label: Constraint first
steps.note: Name the non-negotiable (no daytime restart) BEFORE any fix — it will rule out at least one option. This is the move that separates a decision from a guess.

steps.label: L1 — clear DNS
steps.note: Resolve from BOTH sides. External returns the LB, in-cluster returns the ClusterIP — both resolve, so name resolution is eliminated, not assumed innocent.

steps.label: L3–L6 — clear route + TLS
steps.note: curl -v proves routing + HTTP on the happy path; openssl 'Verify return code: 0' proves the cert chain is trusted. Two layers crossed off with two commands.

steps.label: L7 — reproduce from the FAILING client
steps.note: Run the probe from INSIDE ns B. Exit 28 (timeout) with no HTTP status means the connection dies below L7 — the app is never reached. This is the load-bearing evidence.

steps.label: The drop is named
steps.note: describe networkpolicy shows the from-selector allows team=a only. ns B is labelled team=b → default-deny drops it. Cause proven at the policy layer, not inferred.

steps.label: Decide + reject + verify
steps.note: Selected: add team=b to the from-selector (hot-applies, honours the no-restart constraint). Rejected: Allow-All — it works but destroys the isolation the constraint exists to protect.

ingress-and-services.caption: Six commands walk DNS → route → TLS → HTTP → policy in order; each eliminates a layer until only the drop survives. A reviewer replays them and lands on the same line.

ingress-and-services.text: The senior move is to run the probe from the client that FAILS, not the one that works. Split-horizon DNS, route asymmetry, and per-namespace NetworkPolicy all pass cleanly from the happy path — that is exactly why they survive so long. Curl from your laptop is a comfort check; curl from inside the failing namespace is evidence.

ingress-and-services.question: A reviewer challenges: 'You say the Ingress is fine and it's a policy drop — prove it, don't describe it.' Which piece of evidence actually settles it?
options: A screenshot of the Ingress dashboard showing the service as green and healthy.
A curl -v 200 from your laptop plus 'kubectl get pods' showing all replicas Running.

A timed probe from inside the failing namespace showing a connection timeout (no HTTP status), alongside 'kubectl describe networkpolicy' whose from-selector excludes that namespace — with a before/after re-run after the fix.
A statement that NetworkPolicy is the most common cause of intermittent Kubernetes connectivity issues.
ingress-and-services.explanation: Only option 3 is observable proof on the FAILING path: a timeout with no HTTP status locates the drop below L7, and the describe output names the exact from-selector that excludes the namespace — replayable, and closed by a before/after re-run. Green dashboards (1) and a laptop 200 (2) only exercise the working path; a general claim about frequency (4) is description, not evidence.

ingress-and-services.title: Two incident write-ups, same outage
ingress-and-services.subtitle: 'Reachable for some clients, fails for others.' One debugs the app; one traces the path.

left.label: App-first (weak)
lines: Assumes the handler is dropping requests
Only evidence: curl 200 from the author's laptop
No trace of DNS / TLS / route / policy layers
Never reproduced from the failing client
No rejected option, no constraint, no replay
Recommends a handler rewrite + redeploy
left.verdict: False confidence — cannot be challenged or replayed

right.label: Path-first (gold)
lines: Names the constraint (no daytime restart) first
Traces DNS → route → TLS → HTTP → Service → policy
dig + openssl clear L1–L6; probe reproduces the fail
describe networkpolicy pins the drop to the from-selector
Selected fix vs rejected Allow-All, with why
Before/after probe = executable verification
right.verdict: Inspectable — a reviewer replays it and agrees

ingress-and-services.caption: The gold version survives the reviewer challenge because every claim maps to a command output on the failing path; the weak version only proves the path that already worked.

ingress-and-services.intro: Prove the packet holds — no vibes:
items: You reproduced the failure from the client that FAILS (correct namespace/network), not from a location where it already works. If you only tested the happy path, you have not diagnosed anything.
Every layer you crossed off has an observation attached: dig for DNS, curl -v for route/HTTP, openssl 'Verify return code: 0' for TLS, kubectl describe for policy. No layer is 'assumed fine'.
The constraint is stated BEFORE the fix and rules out at least one plausible option (e.g. Allow-All is rejected because it breaks isolation).
The failure trigger is specific enough to recognise again ('any namespace not in the from-selector'), not 'sometimes it breaks'.
Verification is a before/after re-run of the failing probe — expected 200 after the fix — captured in the packet, and the top-3 residual risks are logged in the risk register.

prompts: Explain why 'reachable for some clients, fails for others' points at the path and almost never at the application code — use your own trace as the example.
Walk the six commands in order and say which layer each one eliminates, and why running the probe from the failing namespace is the load-bearing step.
State your selected fix and the one you rejected, and name the exact constraint that killed the rejected option.

ingress-and-services.text: The same layer-by-layer trace travels to any request path with a hidden hop. A mesh sidecar (mTLS between services) turns the TLS layer into an intra-cluster trust check — an expired sidecar cert fails 'some callers, not others' identically, and openssl on the pod-to-pod path is still the proof. A regulated enterprise adds an egress firewall and split-horizon DNS: the trace gains a route-table and firewall-rule step, but the discipline is invariant — name the constraint, walk DNS → route → TLS → HTTP → Service → policy, reproduce from the failing client, prove the drop. Carry network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md into the capstone unchanged in structure: it is your evidence that you can locate a network fault by layer, not by guessing.

networkpolicy-boundaries.outcome: Take a real (or realistic) Kubernetes service that is reachable from some clients but blocked for others after a NetworkPolicy change, and write the decision packet: the allowed-vs-denied path, the constraint (deny-by-default namespace), the policy you would ship, the policy you rejected, the failure that reappears, and the exact dig/curl/kubectl evidence that proves it.
networkpolicy-boundaries.proof: network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md with: context, the suspect edge on the path (namespace ingress on port 8080), selected policy, rejected policy, expected failure trigger, verification via `kubectl describe networkpolicy` + `curl -v` from an allowed and a denied pod, one reviewer objection answered, and a transfer note. A reviewer can replay the deny and watch your policy flip it to allow.
networkpolicy-boundaries.unlock: Your packet names the constraint before the policy, shows the exact allow/deny path, and attaches at least one inspection-hook output (dig, curl, openssl, or kubectl describe networkpolicy).
networkpolicy-boundaries.doNotClaim: Do not claim the boundary is 'proven' because the manifest applied cleanly. `kubectl apply` succeeding says the YAML parsed, not that the right traffic is allowed and the wrong traffic is denied. Proof is a curl from a pod that SHOULD reach it succeeding, AND a curl from a pod that should NOT reach it timing out — both observed, not assumed.

networkpolicy-boundaries.text: The deploy went out at 14:02, and by 14:05 the payments team is paging: their checkout pods get connection-refused to your service, but your own smoke test from the same namespace passes green. The app didn't change. A deny-by-default NetworkPolicy landed on the namespace and quietly cut every ingress you never explicitly allowed.

In Kubernetes, a NetworkPolicy is a boundary that decides which pods may reach which pods — and the instant one deny-by-default policy selects a namespace, every allow becomes something you must state on purpose. This is release/review risk: the code is innocent, the boundary is the incident.

networkpolicy-boundaries.prompt: Your service works from your own pods but fails from the payments namespace after a policy change. The instinct is to open the app logs and hunt the 500. Before you do — what does that instinct cost you here? Answer before reading on.
networkpolicy-boundaries.reveal: There is no 500 to find. A denied NetworkPolicy connection never reaches your app — the SYN is dropped at the pod network, so your service logs nothing and your traces are empty. Reading app logs is searching the one place the evidence cannot be. The signal lives one layer down: `kubectl describe networkpolicy`, and a `curl -v` from the payments pod that hangs on 'Trying 10.x.x.x…' and times out. Empty app logs + a client-side timeout is the fingerprint of a policy deny, not a bug.

networkpolicy-boundaries.title: A NetworkPolicy boundary is deny-by-default plus every allow stated on purpose
networkpolicy-boundaries.text: The moment a policy selects pods, unlisted ingress is denied. The boundary is correct only when you can name who is allowed, who is denied, and show both — a curl that should pass passing, and a curl that should fail timing out.

networkpolicy-boundaries.title: The blocked path: where the deny happens, and where the repair lands
networkpolicy-boundaries.subtitle: Payments pod → your service on port 8080. The deny-by-default policy on the api namespace drops ingress from unlabeled sources (the failure path, red). The fix is a targeted ingress allow keyed to the payments pod label (the repair path, green). DNS and TLS are on the path but are NOT the cause — marked muted so you don't chase them.

legend.label: failure path — policy drops the SYN, app logs nothing
repair path — a scoped ingress allow, keyed to the pod label
on the path but NOT the cause (DNS/TLS/same-ns) — don't chase

networkpolicy-boundaries.title: The gold artifact: a deny-by-default policy plus one scoped allow
networkpolicy-boundaries.subtitle: network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md ships this manifest. It closes the namespace, then re-opens exactly one ingress — payments pods on 8080 — and nothing else. Label-scoped, not CIDR-guessed.
networkpolicy-boundaries.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: api-default-deny-plus-payments
  namespace: api
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              role: payments
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
# Verify (the proof, not the apply):
#   kubectl describe networkpolicy api-default-deny-plus-payments -n api
#   kubectl exec -n payments deploy/checkout -- curl -v --max-time 5 http://api.api.svc:8080/health   # MUST pass
#   kubectl exec -n default   deploy/scratch  -- curl -v --max-time 5 http://api.api.svc:8080/health   # MUST time out

steps.label: The boundary target
steps.note: podSelector app=api scopes the policy to your service's pods. This is the surface you are drawing a boundary around — get it wrong and you protect the wrong pods.

steps.label: Ingress-only = deny-by-default inbound
steps.note: Listing Ingress in policyTypes flips the default: any inbound not matched below is now DENIED. This single line is what caused the payments outage — and what you're now stating on purpose.

steps.label: The one allow, keyed to a label
steps.note: Allow ingress FROM pods labeled role=payments. Label-scoped, not an IP or CIDR — pods get new IPs on every reschedule, so a CIDR allow rots. This is the rejected-option boundary made concrete.

steps.label: Scope the port too
steps.note: Allow only TCP 8080. An allow with no ports opens every port on the pod — a quiet over-grant a reviewer will catch.

steps.label: Proof #1 — the allowed path passes
steps.note: curl from a payments pod MUST return 200. If it hangs, your podSelector label doesn't match the real pod labels — the classic silent miss.

steps.label: Proof #2 — the denied path times out
steps.note: curl from an unlisted namespace MUST time out, not refuse. A timeout (dropped SYN) is the signature of a working deny; a fast connection-refused means the policy isn't selecting the pod at all.

networkpolicy-boundaries.caption: The boundary is proven when line 21 passes AND line 22 times out. One without the other is half a proof: open-to-everyone, or closed-to-everyone.

networkpolicy-boundaries.title: Two 'fixes' for the payments outage
networkpolicy-boundaries.subtitle: Both make payments work again. Only one is a defensible boundary a reviewer signs.

left.label: Debug the app, then blanket-allow
lines: Spent 40 min in api app logs — found nothing (there was nothing)
Assumed DNS: ran dig, it resolved fine — still stuck
'Fix': ingress with empty from → allow ALL namespaces
curl from payments passes; curl from anywhere ALSO passes
No deny proof — never tested a pod that should be blocked
Allow has no ports → every port on the pod is open
left.verdict: Reopens the outage by deleting the boundary

right.label: Trace the path, scope the allow
lines: Empty app logs + client timeout → read it as a policy deny
kubectl describe networkpolicy → confirmed no allow matched payments
Fix: allow FROM podSelector role=payments, port 8080 only
curl from payments passes (200); curl from default times out
Both proofs captured in the packet — allow AND deny observed
Rejected CIDR allow: pod IPs churn, so it silently rots
right.verdict: Boundary holds — allowed passes, denied drops, provably

networkpolicy-boundaries.caption: The weak fix confuses 'payments can reach it' with 'the policy is correct.' The gold fix proves the deny still bites — the half of the boundary the outage made everyone forget.

networkpolicy-boundaries.text: The senior tell in Kubernetes networking: a deny is a timeout, a missing service is a refuse. A dropped SYN from a NetworkPolicy makes the client hang until timeout; a wrong port or absent endpoint returns connection-refused immediately. If your 'blocked' pod gets refused fast, the policy isn't even selecting the target — you're debugging the wrong layer. Read the failure mode before you write the allow.

networkpolicy-boundaries.question: A reviewer challenges your NetworkPolicy: 'You proved payments can reach the service. Show me it's actually a boundary and not just open.' What is the exact evidence that answers them?
options: The output of `kubectl apply` showing the policy was created successfully.
A `curl -v` from a payments pod returning 200, plus a `curl -v` from an unlisted namespace pod timing out — both captured against the same service.
A screenshot of the YAML manifest with the ingress rule highlighted.
A `dig` showing the service name resolves to a ClusterIP.
networkpolicy-boundaries.explanation: A boundary is two claims — allowed traffic passes AND denied traffic is dropped — so it takes two observations. Only option 2 shows both: the allowed path returning 200 and the denied path timing out. `apply` (1) proves the YAML parsed, the manifest (3) proves intent not effect, and `dig` (4) proves DNS, which was never the cause. The deny half is the part the outage made everyone forget to test.

networkpolicy-boundaries.intro: Prove your boundary holds — no vibes, three layers of proof:
items: Decision proof: your packet names the constraint (deny-by-default on ns=api) BEFORE the policy, and states the rejected option (a CIDR-based allow) with why it rots — pod IPs change on reschedule.

Operational proof — allow side: `kubectl exec` a curl from a pod that SHOULD reach the service returns 200. If it hangs, your podSelector label doesn't match the real pod labels; run `kubectl get pod --show-labels` and reconcile.
Operational proof — deny side: `kubectl exec` a curl from a pod that should NOT reach it TIMES OUT (not refuses). A fast refuse means the policy isn't selecting your target pods at all.

Read the boundary back from the cluster: `kubectl describe networkpolicy` shows exactly one allowed source and one allowed port — no empty `from` (which allows all) and no empty `ports` (which opens every port).

Transfer proof: name what changes in a stricter environment (a regulated cluster adds egress deny + DNS-only allow, so CoreDNS itself needs an explicit egress rule or every pod loses name resolution).

prompts: Explain why empty app logs plus a client-side timeout points at a NetworkPolicy deny and not an application bug — trace where the SYN dies.
Your reviewer asks why you keyed the allow to a pod label instead of the payments pods' IP range. Answer using your own packet.
Walk the difference between a connection that TIMES OUT and one that is REFUSED, and what each tells you about whether the policy is selecting the right pods.

networkpolicy-boundaries.text: This is the whole shape of release/review risk in cloud networking: the code is fine, the boundary is the incident, and the proof is a path traced — not a log read. The same move carries to a security-group change on a cloud load balancer (an allow-list edit silently drops a health check), to a firewall rule in front of an API (asymmetric routing lets the request in but blocks the reply), and to a service mesh's authorization policy (mTLS trusts the caller but the AuthorizationPolicy still denies the route). Everywhere a boundary decides who may reach whom, the expert proves BOTH halves — allowed passes, denied drops — and never confuses 'my traffic works' with 'the boundary is correct.' Carry network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md into the capstone: it is the reusable evidence that you can trace a path, break a boundary, and repair it under review.

packet-capture-plan.outcome: Take a real intermittent-reachability failure — a service that works for some clients but fails for others after a DNS, TLS, routing, or policy change — and write a Packet Capture Plan: WHERE you will tap, the exact BPF filter, the single hypothesis each capture kills, and the boundary you will not cross. Then commit it to network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md.
packet-capture-plan.proof: The 'Capture Plan' section of network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md: at least two capture points on the path (client-side, LB, pod/host), a scoped BPF filter for each (host/port, not 'capture everything'), the hypothesis each tap disqualifies, and an explicit stop rule. A reviewer agrees your FIRST capture is the one most likely to prove where the path breaks — DNS, TLS, route, or policy — for the least data.
packet-capture-plan.unlock: Your plan names the capture points, a scoped filter per point, the hypothesis each kills, and a boundary you will not tap — before you run a single tcpdump.
packet-capture-plan.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a capture plan if it is just 'run tcpdump on the box'. An unscoped, single-point capture on one machine is a hope, not a plan. A plan taps BOTH sides of the suspect edge so the packet either arrives or it does not — that is the whole point.

packet-capture-plan.text: It is hour three of a P1: checkout works from the office VPN and fails from half the mobile users, and someone already 'fixed' the app code twice. A staff SRE ignores the code, opens two terminals, and runs one tcpdump at the load balancer and one inside the pod — and in ninety seconds proves the SYN never reaches the pod. The bug was a NetworkPolicy, not a line of code.

Intermittent reachability after a DNS, TLS, routing, or policy change is the classic trap: the symptom looks like application code, but the cause lives in name resolution, certificate trust, route asymmetry, or a firewall rule. A capture plan decides WHERE to put the tap so the packets tell you which layer actually broke — this is Section 1 of the incident packet you carry through this module.

packet-capture-plan.prompt: A service fails for ~40% of clients after a rollout. Your first instinct is to run `tcpdump -i any` on the affected pod and read the trace. Before you do — what is wrong with starting there? Answer before reading on.
packet-capture-plan.reveal: A single capture on ONE end can only tell you what arrived, never what was sent. If the pod sees no SYN, you cannot tell 'the client never sent it' from 'a route/NAT/NetworkPolicy dropped it in flight' — the two failures look identical from one tap. The senior move is to capture on BOTH sides of the suspect edge at once: `tcpdump host <client> and port 443` at the LB AND in the pod. The packet either crosses the edge or it does not — and now the drop point is proven, not guessed.

packet-capture-plan.title: A capture plan taps both sides of the suspect edge, scoped and hypothesis-first
packet-capture-plan.text: Pick the edge the diagnosis suspects, tap on BOTH sides simultaneously, scope each tap with a tight BPF filter (host + port), and name the hypothesis each capture kills. The invariant: a captured packet is evidence a drop is not — it proves which layer broke.

packet-capture-plan.title: Where to tap on the request path
packet-capture-plan.subtitle: One request crosses five trust boundaries: DNS, TLS handshake, LB, NetworkPolicy, pod. Each has a layer that can silently break it. The capture plan taps BEFORE and AFTER the suspect edge (LB → NetworkPolicy → pod) so a dropped SYN is caught where it dies. Auth and billing are deliberately out of scope.

nodes.label: Service Pod
nodes.description: TAP #2 — does SYN cross the policy?

legend.label: capture points (both sides of the edge)
layers that fail silently: DNS, TLS, policy
kept out of scope on purpose

packet-capture-plan.title: Writing the Capture Plan, one line at a time
packet-capture-plan.subtitle: The plan section in network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md — scoped BPF filters, paired taps, a hypothesis per capture.
packet-capture-plan.code:
## 1. Capture Plan  (service: checkout.svc, symptom: works for VPN, fails for ~40% mobile after policy change)
# Confirm resolution first — is DNS even returning the right VIP for failing clients?
dig +short checkout.example.com            # kill-test: split-horizon / stale record
# TAP #1 — load balancer: does the client SYN + TLS ClientHello arrive at all?
tcpdump -ni eth0 'host 203.0.113.10 and tcp port 443' -c 200 -w lb.pcap
# TAP #2 — inside the pod: does that same SYN cross the NetworkPolicy?
kubectl debug -it checkout-pod --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- \
  tcpdump -ni eth0 'tcp port 8443 and tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0' -c 50 -w pod.pcap
# Boundary: do NOT tap the billing path or capture unfiltered 'any' (PII + noise).
# Stop rule: SYN in lb.pcap but absent in pod.pcap -> NetworkPolicy drop, decide. Or 15 min.

steps.label: Frame the capture
steps.note: Name the service, the symptom, and the recent change (policy) in the header. A capture with no hypothesis is a data dump.

steps.label: Rule out DNS first — cheapest layer
steps.note: dig is a two-second kill-test. Split-horizon DNS or a stale record explains 'some clients fail' before any packet capture. If the VIP is wrong, stop here.

steps.label: TAP #1 at the LB — scoped to host + port
steps.note: 'host <client> and tcp port 443' — NOT 'tcpdump -i any'. The filter proves the ClientHello arrives at the edge, and keeps the pcap small and PII-bounded.

steps.label: TAP #2 in the pod — the SAME flow, the other side
steps.note: kubectl debug + netshoot taps inside the pod netns. The tcp-syn filter isolates connection setup. If the SYN is in lb.pcap but not here, the NetworkPolicy dropped it — silently, exactly as they do.

steps.label: The boundary
steps.note: Never capture unfiltered on a shared node: it sweeps up other tenants' traffic (PII, secrets in flight). Scope every tap, and name what you will NOT tap.

steps.label: The stop rule
steps.note: SYN present upstream + absent downstream = proven drop point. A concrete threshold turns 'keep capturing' into 'decide'.

packet-capture-plan.caption: Run both taps against one failing client at once: SYN lands in lb.pcap, never appears in pod.pcap — the NetworkPolicy is the drop, proven with two filters and no code changes.

packet-capture-plan.title: A hope vs a capture plan
packet-capture-plan.subtitle: Same incident: 'checkout fails for ~40% of clients after a rollout.' Both involve tcpdump; only one localizes the drop.

left.label: One unscoped capture, one side
lines: tcpdump -i any on the pod, no filter
Sees nothing arrive — but SENT is unknown
Cannot separate 'client never sent' from 'dropped in flight'
Sweeps up other tenants' traffic (PII risk)
No DNS/TLS check — assumes it's the app
No stop rule: capture runs until someone gives up
left.verdict: Proves nothing — a data dump with a hunch

right.label: Paired, scoped, hypothesis-first
lines: dig first — kill split-horizon/stale DNS cheaply
TAP #1 at LB + TAP #2 in pod, same flow, at once
BPF scoped to host + port on each side
SYN in lb.pcap, absent in pod.pcap = policy drop, proven
Boundary: billing path + unfiltered 'any' out of scope
Stop rule: drop localized OR 15 min → decide
right.verdict: Localizes the break to a layer — DNS, TLS, route, or policy

packet-capture-plan.caption: The signal is the DIFFERENCE between the two captures. One tap can only show absence; a packet present upstream and absent downstream turns 'it's flaky' into 'the NetworkPolicy drops it here.'

packet-capture-plan.text: The senior tell: they capture on both sides of the suspect edge BEFORE touching code, and they scope every filter to a host and port. 'Works for VPN, fails for mobile' is almost never the application — it is asymmetric routing, split-horizon DNS, an SNI/cert mismatch on the TLS ClientHello, or a NetworkPolicy that only allows the VPN CIDR. The packets say which one; the code review never will.

packet-capture-plan.question: A reviewer challenges: 'You captured on the pod and saw no SYN — so the client is broken, right?' Why is that conclusion unproven, and what capture plan proves it?
options: It is proven — no SYN at the pod means the client never sent one; close the ticket on the client team.

A single downstream capture cannot distinguish 'never sent' from 'dropped in flight'. Capture the SAME flow on both sides — LB and pod — so a SYN present at the LB but absent in the pod localizes the drop to the NetworkPolicy or route between them.
Re-run `tcpdump -i any` for longer on the pod until a SYN eventually shows up.
Skip captures and add more application logging, since the pod is clearly the problem.
packet-capture-plan.explanation: One tap only tells you what arrived at that tap — absence at the pod is consistent with BOTH a client that never sent and an in-flight drop (NetworkPolicy, NAT, asymmetric route). The plan that proves it captures the same flow on both sides of the suspect edge: SYN present upstream + absent downstream isolates the drop to that segment. Options 1 and 4 assume the answer; option 3 just adds noise.

packet-capture-plan.intro: Prove your Capture Plan is executable and inspectable — no vibes:
items: Every capture point names an interface AND a scoped BPF filter (host + port). If any tap is `-i any` with no filter, tighten it — an unscoped capture is a PII and noise liability, not evidence.
At least one cheap non-capture check (dig / curl -v / openssl s_client) runs FIRST to rule out DNS resolution or TLS trust before you reach for tcpdump.
The plan taps BOTH sides of the suspect edge for the same flow, so a packet present-then-absent localizes the drop — a single-sided capture cannot.
Each capture states the hypothesis it kills (DNS, TLS handshake, route/NAT, or NetworkPolicy) — a capture with no hypothesis is a data dump.
A boundary is written down: at least one path or interface you will NOT tap, and why (out of scope / tenant PII).
A stop rule with a concrete threshold exists (drop localized OR a time box), so capturing cannot run forever.

prompts: In your own words: why can a single tcpdump on one host never distinguish 'the client never sent the packet' from 'something dropped it in flight' — and what does a paired capture add?
Walk through your own plan: which layer does each capture point kill (DNS, TLS, route, NetworkPolicy), and why is that the cheapest order to run them in?
Defend one boundary in your plan — a path or interface you deliberately did NOT tap. Why is leaving it out a judgment, not an oversight?

packet-capture-plan.text: This is not a Kubernetes trick — it is the diagnostic move for any layered path with a hidden drop. A network engineer captures at both ends of a WAN link to localize loss to one hop; a support engineer runs `dig` and `openssl s_client` before blaming an API; a mobile team taps at the CDN edge and the origin to find where a request dies. Anywhere a request crosses trust boundaries and 'works for some, fails for others,' the plan is the same: rule out DNS and TLS cheaply, then tap both sides of the suspect edge, scoped and hypothesis-first. Next you carry this exact incident packet forward — the capture plan becomes the evidence that the fix (loosen the NetworkPolicy CIDR, not touch the app) is proven, not guessed. Keep network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md; you will reuse it in the capstone.

firewall-denial-repair.outcome: Take a real (or realistic) 'works for some clients, denied for others' incident and produce network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md: the constraint, the traced path, the selected repair, the rejected option, the failure trigger, and the exact dig/curl/openssl/NetworkPolicy evidence that proves the denial was a FIREWALL/policy decision — not application code.
firewall-denial-repair.proof: network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md with a path trace (DNS → route → TLS → policy), the suspect edge named, one inspection-hook output showing the denial, the chosen repair, the rejected option and why it fails, and one reviewer objection answered. A peer can replay the denial from your evidence without you narrating.
firewall-denial-repair.unlock: Your packet names the constraint, shows the denial at a specific edge with real command output, and states the repair plus the rejected alternative — with zero application-code changes proposed.
firewall-denial-repair.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'repaired the firewall' if your evidence only shows the app returning an error. An app-level 500 or timeout is a symptom, not proof of a policy denial. The proof is a packet/connection that never completes at a specific hop — SYN with no SYN-ACK, a policy that selects the pod, a rule that drops the CIDR. No dropped-connection evidence, no repair.

firewall-denial-repair.text: The service is green on the dashboard, healthy from the office VPN, and dead from the new region — and three engineers are already rewriting the retry logic. The denial isn't in the code they're editing; it's a firewall rule that never let the packet arrive.

A production service reachable from some clients but denied for others is almost never an application bug — it's name resolution, certificate trust, route asymmetry, or network policy. This lesson turns that intermittent denial into a traced, evidenced repair packet you carry into the capstone.

firewall-denial-repair.prompt: curl to the service hangs and eventually times out from Region B, but works instantly from Region A. Your teammate says 'the app is slow, add a timeout retry.' Before you agree — what's wrong with that read?
firewall-denial-repair.reveal: A hang-then-timeout is the signature of a silent DROP, not a slow app. A busy app REJECTS fast (connection refused / 500 in milliseconds) or answers late — it does not black-hole. When the TCP handshake never completes (SYN sent, no SYN-ACK) for one CIDR but not another, a firewall or NetworkPolicy is dropping the packet before your code ever runs. Adding retries just makes the denial slower to surface.

firewall-denial-repair.title: Trace the path, prove the drop, repair the rule — not the code
firewall-denial-repair.text: A firewall denial repair traces DNS → route → TLS → policy to the exact edge where the connection dies, proves the drop with command output (not an app error), then repairs the offending rule. The invariant: repair the policy that denied the packet, never the application that never saw it.

firewall-denial-repair.title: The request path — where a denial hides at each hop
firewall-denial-repair.subtitle: Client → DNS → route → firewall/NetworkPolicy → TLS → pod. The denial for Region B lives on the policy edge (gateway firewall drops the CIDR); the app is reached only if the packet survives every prior hop. Region A's CIDR is allowlisted, so it passes.

nodes.label: Service pod
nodes.description: app code — only runs if packet arrives

legend.label: the denial: silent drop of Region B's CIDR
app code — never reached, not the cause

firewall-denial-repair.title: Proving the denial — dig, curl, openssl, then the NetworkPolicy
firewall-denial-repair.subtitle: The inspection hooks, run in path order, until the drop is located and named. This is the evidence block of the packet.
firewall-denial-repair.code:
# 1. DNS resolves fine from Region B — rule out name resolution
dig +short service.example.com
# 203.0.113.10   → same IP as Region A. DNS is NOT the denial.

# 2. curl hangs, then times out — the drop signature (no fast reject)
curl -v --connect-timeout 5 https://service.example.com/health
# * Trying 203.0.113.10:443...
# * Connection timed out after 5001 ms   ← SYN sent, no SYN-ACK = silent DROP

# 3. Confirm it dies BEFORE TLS — openssl can't even open the socket
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 -servername service.example.com
# connect: Connection timed out   ← never reached the TLS layer

# 4. Find the policy that selects the pod and omits Region B's CIDR
kubectl describe networkpolicy allow-ingress -n prod
# Spec:
#   PodSelector: app=orders
#   Ingress:
#     From: ipBlock 10.10.0.0/16 (Region A)   ← Region B 10.40.0.0/16 MISSING
#   default: DROP everything not explicitly allowed

steps.label: Rule out DNS first
steps.note: dig returns the same IP from both regions — name resolution is not the denial. Eliminating the cheapest suspect first keeps the trace honest.

steps.label: curl reveals the drop signature
steps.note: '-v' with a short --connect-timeout: a HANG then timeout means SYN sent, no SYN-ACK. That black-hole is a firewall DROP, not a slow app. A busy app would refuse or answer, not vanish.

steps.label: openssl confirms it dies before TLS
steps.note: The socket never opens, so this is not a certificate or SNI problem. The denial is below TLS — at the routing/policy layer.

steps.label: Name the offending rule
steps.note: The NetworkPolicy selects app=orders and allows only Region A's ipBlock; the default-deny drops Region B's 10.40.0.0/16. This is the suspect edge, now proven — the repair is to add the missing CIDR, scoped to the needed ports.

firewall-denial-repair.caption: Four hooks, in path order, converge on one rule. The evidence is a connection that never completes at a named policy — not an app error log. That is the difference between 'described' and 'proven'.

firewall-denial-repair.title: Weak repair vs proven repair
firewall-denial-repair.subtitle: Same incident: 'service denied for Region B clients.' One is a guess dressed as a fix; one is an evidenced, scoped repair.

left.label: Debug the app (weak)
lines: Symptom read as 'app is slow' → added retry + longer timeout
No path trace: DNS, route, TLS never checked
No drop evidence — only the app's own timeout log
'Fix': redeploy the orders service (untouched cause)
Or the blunt over-fix: allow 0.0.0.0/0 to make it 'work'
left.verdict: Never saw the packet — denial persists or security hole opened

right.label: Trace, prove, scope (gold)
lines: Traced DNS → route → TLS → policy; ruled out each cheap suspect
curl hang + openssl timeout = drop proven below TLS
kubectl describe names the rule: Region B CIDR omitted
Repair: add 10.40.0.0/16 to ingress, ports 443 only (least-privilege)
Verify: curl from Region B returns 200; rejected 0.0.0.0/0 as over-broad
right.verdict: Denial located, repaired at the rule, and re-verified

firewall-denial-repair.caption: The gold repair is scoped: it opens exactly the CIDR and port the trace proved were denied — never 'allow all' to make the red turn green. A repair that widens the blast radius is a new incident.

firewall-denial-repair.text: The senior tell: the first move on 'works for some, fails for others' is to trace the path and eliminate DNS, route, and TLS before touching the app. Anyone can add allow-all and watch the dashboard go green — that's not a repair, it's deferring a breach. A NetworkPolicy default-denies everything not explicitly allowed, so the real skill is naming the exact CIDR/port the trace proved you need, and defending why nothing wider.

firewall-denial-repair.question: A reviewer challenges your packet: 'How do I know this was a firewall denial and not the application failing?' Which single piece of evidence answers that?
options: The application log shows a 500 error and a stack trace for the failed request.

curl -v hangs and times out at the TCP connect stage (SYN, no SYN-ACK) from the denied CIDR while succeeding from the allowed one, and kubectl describe networkpolicy shows that CIDR is not in the ingress allowlist.
The dashboard shows elevated latency for the affected region.
Restarting the pod temporarily made the errors go away.
firewall-denial-repair.explanation: Only option 2 proves a policy-layer denial: the connection dies before TLS (so the app never ran), it fails only for the denied CIDR, and the offending rule is named. An app 500 (1) means the packet DID arrive — the opposite conclusion. Latency (3) and a pod restart (4) are symptoms that don't distinguish a drop from an app fault.

items: Your packet traces the path in order (DNS → route → TLS → policy) and eliminates each cheap suspect with an inspection-hook output, not a hunch.
The denial is shown as a connection that never completes (curl hang/timeout or openssl connect failure) from the denied source — while the same command succeeds from an allowed source.
The offending rule is named: the exact firewall entry or NetworkPolicy ipBlock, and the specific CIDR/port that was missing.
The repair is least-privilege: it adds only the CIDR and ports the trace proved were denied. You can state which broader option (e.g. 0.0.0.0/0) you rejected and why.
Post-repair re-verification is attached: the same curl from the previously denied client now returns 200, and the allowed client still works (no regression).

prompts: Explain, from memory, why a hang-then-timeout is evidence of a firewall DROP but a fast connection-refused or a 500 is not.
Walk the path DNS → route → TLS → policy for your own incident and name the exact hop where the denial lived and how you proved it.
Your repair added a CIDR to the allowlist. Which broader rule did you reject, and how would you defend the scope you chose to a security reviewer?

firewall-denial-repair.text: This is path-tracing under denial, and it travels. A regulated enterprise pushes the same repair through a change ticket with an egress-firewall CIDR review instead of a kubectl edit; a high-scale product finds the denial is a per-region security group or a mTLS SNI mismatch, not a NetworkPolicy — same trace, different offending rule. What stays invariant: prove the drop at a named edge, repair the policy not the app, and scope the allowlist to exactly what the evidence demanded. The network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md you just built is capstone evidence — the incident where you traced, proved, repaired, and re-verified a denial. Carry it forward: the capstone reuses this exact packet and its proof.

zero-trust-access.outcome: Take a real request-path incident — a service reachable for some clients but failing for others after a DNS, TLS, routing, or NetworkPolicy change — and write network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md that proves, with dig/curl/openssl/kubectl evidence, WHERE trust actually breaks, not where you assumed it did.
zero-trust-access.proof: network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md with: context, the operating constraint, selected approach, rejected approach, the layer where trust broke (name resolution | certificate trust | route asymmetry | NetworkPolicy), a verification trail (at least two of dig / curl -v / openssl s_client / kubectl describe networkpolicy), the reviewer objection, and a transfer note. A second reviewer can replay the failure and confirm the repair.
zero-trust-access.unlock: Your packet names the exact layer trust broke on, backed by inspection-hook output — not an application-code guess — and states what evidence would INVALIDATE the finding.
zero-trust-access.doNotClaim: Do not claim 'zero-trust access is enforced' because a request succeeded from your laptop. A pass from one client on one network proves that path, not the policy. Until you show a deny that SHOULD deny and an allow that SHOULD allow — each with hook output — you have a demo, not a verified access boundary.

zero-trust-access.text: The service is green on your machine and paging in production: half the clients get 200s, the other half hang, and three engineers are already deep in the application code — where the bug is not. The real break is one layer down: a name that resolves differently, a cert nobody trusts, a route that only goes one way, or a NetworkPolicy that quietly denies the pod.

Zero-trust means every hop re-verifies identity and authorization instead of trusting the network — so a failure is never 'the network is down', it is a specific hop refusing a specific caller. This lesson closes Network Debugging & Security: it turns 'it works for me' into an inspectable decision packet that survives a reviewer replaying your evidence.

zero-trust-access.prompt: A production service works from the office network but fails from the new cluster. Before touching code, what is the single fastest first move — and why would testing the application logic be a trap?
zero-trust-access.reveal: Trace the path, do not read the code. Zero-trust adds re-verification at every hop, so 'works here, fails there' is almost always a hop-specific trust decision: the new cluster resolves the name to a different IP, presents a client cert the server does not trust, takes a route the return path never mirrors, or lives in a namespace a NetworkPolicy denies. `dig` + `curl -v` + `kubectl describe networkpolicy` from the FAILING client localizes the break in minutes; re-reading application code confirms only that the code you own is innocent — which you already suspected.

zero-trust-access.title: Trust is re-checked at every hop — so debug the path, not the app
zero-trust-access.text: Zero-trust removes implicit network trust: each hop re-verifies identity (mTLS cert) and authorization (policy) for each caller. A break is one hop denying one caller. Localize it along the path — name → cert → route → policy — with observable evidence before changing anything.

zero-trust-access.title: The zero-trust request path — where trust is granted, and where it breaks
zero-trust-access.subtitle: Client → DNS → route → mTLS handshake → NetworkPolicy admission → pod. Each hop RE-VERIFIES. The failure path (a denied caller) and the repair path (an allowed, proven caller) run through the same four checkpoints.

nodes.label: Trust denied
nodes.description: wrong IP · untrusted cert · asymmetric route · policy deny

legend.label: failure path — trust denied at a hop

zero-trust-access.caption: The application code sits behind the pod. Every dashed edge is a break the app can never explain — and every solid accent edge is a hook you can run to localize it.

zero-trust-access.title: The verification trail inside network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md
zero-trust-access.subtitle: The real artifact: run each hook FROM THE FAILING CLIENT, paste output, and the break localizes itself. This is the Build deliverable, filled.
zero-trust-access.code:
# Verification trail — run from the FAILING client, not your laptop

# Hop 1 — Name resolution: does the name point where I think?
$ dig +short api.internal.svc
10.4.7.22        # office resolver -> old IP; cluster resolver -> 10.8.3.9 (DRIFT)

# Hop 2 — Route / TLS reachability: can I even open the socket + who answers?
$ curl -v --connect-timeout 5 https://api.internal.svc/health
*   Trying 10.8.3.9:443...
* SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate  # cert not trusted

# Hop 3 — Certificate trust: whose CA signed this, and is it expired?
$ openssl s_client -connect 10.8.3.9:443 -servername api.internal.svc </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -dates
issuer=CN=mesh-ca-2023          # rotated CA; failing clients still trust mesh-ca-2022
notAfter=Jun 30 00:00:00 2026 GMT

# Hop 4 — Authorization: does policy actually admit this caller's namespace/labels?
$ kubectl describe networkpolicy api-allow -n prod
Ingress: From: podSelector app=gateway   # allows gateway pods ONLY
# failing client is app=batch-runner -> no matching allow rule -> DENY

# Finding: two independent breaks -> resolver drift (Hop 1) AND policy deny (Hop 4)

steps.label: Hop 1 — resolve from the failing client
steps.note: dig +short from the failing network, not yours. Same name, two answers = resolver/split-horizon drift. This alone explains 'works for some clients'.

steps.label: Hop 2 — one curl -v spans route + TLS
steps.note: 'Trying <IP>' confirms the route opened; the SSL line localizes the break to certificate trust, not the app. curl -v is the cheapest disqualifier on the path.

steps.label: Hop 3 — name the CA, don't guess
steps.note: openssl prints issuer + dates. A rotated CA (2022 -> 2023) that failing clients never got is the classic zero-trust break: identity, not connectivity.

steps.label: Hop 4 — read the policy, don't assume
steps.note: kubectl describe networkpolicy shows the ACTUAL allow rule. app=gateway only means app=batch-runner is denied by default-deny — a policy decision, invisible to the application.

steps.label: The finding is a layer, backed by output
steps.note: Two independent breaks. The packet records BOTH with evidence; a reviewer replays each hook and confirms. This is operational proof, not description.

zero-trust-access.caption: Each hook can return 'no' and eliminate a hop — that is what makes the trail falsifiable. The invalidation condition: if the failing client's dig, cert, and policy all match a passing client's, the break is elsewhere.

zero-trust-access.title: Weak packet vs gold packet — the same incident
zero-trust-access.subtitle: Worked Expert Example: one describes zero-trust, one proves where trust broke. Only the gold packet survives a reviewer replaying it.

left.label: Weak — described, not proven
lines: 'Zero-trust access is configured, service should be reachable'
Debugged application code for two hours
No dig / curl / openssl / kubectl output attached
Never states the operating constraint (no daytime downtime)
No rejected option, no failure trigger, no invalidation condition
Reviewer cannot replay it or point to a denied hop
left.verdict: False confidence — passes review, fails when the evidence changes

right.label: Gold — network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md
lines: Constraint named: fix live, no daytime downtime on the prod path
Break localized to two hops with hook output (resolver drift + policy deny)
Selected: push CA bundle + add batch-runner allow rule; Rejected: disable mTLS (breaks zero-trust)
Failure trigger recorded: caller in a namespace with no allow rule

Reviewer replays every hook and confirms the deny, then the allow

zero-trust-access.caption: The weak version cannot be challenged, so it cannot be trusted. The gold version invites the challenge and answers it with output — that is the entire premium bar for this lesson.

zero-trust-access.text: The zero-trust tell that separates operators from guessers: default-deny is not a bug, it is the design. When a caller fails, the senior move is 'which allow rule was it missing, and should it exist?' — not 'the network is blocking us'. A NetworkPolicy denying an unlisted caller is the system working; the question is whether that caller earned an allow, proven by identity, not by IP range.

zero-trust-access.question: A reviewer challenges: 'You say zero-trust access works — prove it, don't describe it.' Which single piece of evidence actually proves it?
options: A screenshot of the service returning 200 from your laptop on the office VPN.
The NetworkPolicy YAML committed to the repo, showing an allow rule exists.
Paired hook output: a caller that SHOULD be denied getting denied (kubectl/openssl), AND the intended caller getting allowed — each replayable from the failing/passing client.
A statement that mTLS is enabled mesh-wide and all pods have sidecars.
zero-trust-access.explanation: Zero-trust is an authorization boundary, so proof is a boundary test: the deny that should deny AND the allow that should allow, each with replayable evidence (openssl for identity, kubectl describe networkpolicy for authorization). A 200 from one trusted client (1) proves one happy path. Committed YAML (2) proves intent, not enforcement. 'mTLS is on' (4) is a description. Only paired, replayable allow/deny output is inspectable proof.

zero-trust-access.intro: Prove your packet — no vibes. Run each from the FAILING client:
items: dig +short the service name from the failing client AND a passing client. If the IPs differ, you have resolver/split-horizon drift — record both answers.

curl -v the health endpoint from the failing client. Confirm you can distinguish a route failure ('Trying <IP>' never completes) from a TLS failure (SSL line) from an app failure (got an HTTP status).
openssl s_client the endpoint and print issuer + notAfter. Confirm the failing client trusts the CA that actually signed the cert, and the cert is unexpired.
kubectl describe networkpolicy for the target namespace. Point to the exact allow rule that admits (or fails to admit) your caller's labels — name it, do not summarize it.
State the invalidation condition explicitly: what identical evidence between a passing and failing client would prove the break is NOT on the path you named.

prompts: In your own words: why does 'it works from my laptop' prove almost nothing about a zero-trust access boundary?
Walk the four hops (DNS → route/TLS → cert → NetworkPolicy) and name the one inspection hook that localizes a break at each, using your own incident.
Explain the difference between a description of zero-trust and a proof of it — cite the exact hook output in your packet that makes it a proof.

zero-trust-access.text: Same discipline, stricter blast radius. In a small team, one shared CA and a handful of allow rules — you can hold the whole path in your head. In a regulated enterprise, every hop needs an audit trail: the packet's hook output becomes the evidence an auditor replays, and 'default-deny + an approved allow rule per caller' is the control being tested. At high scale, resolver drift and CA rotation are continuous, not incidents, so the packet becomes a runbook: same four hops, same hooks, run on a schedule. What stays invariant everywhere — trust is re-verified per hop, and a break is one hop denying one caller, provable with dig/curl/openssl/kubectl. This packet is your capstone evidence: not 'I understand zero-trust' but 'here is an access failure I localized to a hop, repaired, and proved — replay it.'

network-incident-runbook.outcome: Trace a partial-outage down the real path — DNS, route, TLS, policy — instead of blaming app code, then commit a decision packet a second reviewer can replay: the constraint, the suspect layer, the fix, and the proof it holds.
network-incident-runbook.proof: network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md: constraint table, suspect layer with dig/curl/openssl evidence, selected fix, rejected option, blast radius, one reviewer objection answered — plus network_incident_runbook_risk_register.md naming the top three residual risks.
network-incident-runbook.unlock: Your packet names the layer BEFORE the fix, attaches at least two inspection-hook outputs, and states what result would invalidate the diagnosis.
network-incident-runbook.doNotClaim: Not a runbook if you 'restarted the pod and it worked.' The skill is separating a network cause from an application symptom — and proving which one it was.

network-incident-runbook.text: The service is green on your laptop and 500ing for half the fleet — and the room is already three commits deep into the app code. The outage is not in the app. It is on an arrow between two boxes, and nobody has traced the arrow.

You mapped systems and read routes in earlier lessons; the incident runbook is where that reasoning meets a live partial outage. The failure that ends careers here is debugging application code while the real fault is name resolution, certificate trust, route asymmetry, or a network policy.

network-incident-runbook.prompt: A production endpoint works for some clients and fails for others right after a deploy. Where do you look first — the application logs, or somewhere earlier on the path?
network-incident-runbook.reveal: Earlier. 'Some clients, not others' is the signature of a network cause, not an app bug — app bugs usually fail for everyone or no one. Split traffic points at DNS returning different records, a route that is asymmetric, a TLS SAN mismatch on one host, or a NetworkPolicy that only some pods hit. Trace the path before you touch the code.

network-incident-runbook.title: Trace the path top-to-bottom before you change the system
network-incident-runbook.text: Walk one request down the layers — DNS resolves, route reaches, TLS trusts, HTTP answers — and stop at the first layer that lies. Name that layer, its blast radius, and the evidence, before proposing any fix.

network-incident-runbook.title: The request path — and where it can lie
network-incident-runbook.subtitle: One request from client to service, layer by layer. Each hop is a place the outage can hide: DNS resolution, IP routing, TLS trust, then HTTP. The decision fork asks 'did this layer answer honestly?' — the suspect edge (TLS trust on one host) is marked, and the blast radius is a subset of clients getting a cert error.
network-incident-runbook.caption: Diagnose layer by layer. The first hop that lies is the cause; everything downstream is a symptom.

network-incident-runbook.title: Four hooks that isolate the layer
network-incident-runbook.subtitle: The real inspection sequence — each command interrogates exactly one layer, so the first failure names the cause.
network-incident-runbook.code:
# Layer 1 — DNS: what IP does THIS client resolve to?
dig +short service.example.com
# → 10.0.4.7   (a healthy client resolves 10.0.5.9 — split answer!)

# Layer 2 — Route + policy: can we even reach the host?
kubectl describe networkpolicy allow-orders | grep -A2 Ingress
# → from: podSelector app=web   (curl client isn't 'web' → denied)

# Layer 3 — TLS: is the cert trusted and does the SAN match?
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 -servername service.example.com </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E 'subject=|Verify'
# → subject=CN=old.example.com   Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify)

# Layer 4 — HTTP: only now, ask the app
curl -v https://service.example.com/health
# → * SSL certificate problem  (fails BEFORE any app code runs)

steps.label: DNS first
steps.note: dig +short shows the record THIS client gets. A split answer (different IPs per client) explains 'some clients fail' without touching the app.

steps.label: Route + policy
steps.note: kubectl describe networkpolicy reveals a podSelector that admits 'web' but not your test pod — asymmetric reachability, not an app fault.

steps.label: TLS trust
steps.note: openssl s_client exposes the cert subject and verify code. Return code 21 with a stale CN is a SAN mismatch — the handshake fails before HTTP exists.

steps.label: HTTP last
steps.note: curl -v fails at 'SSL certificate problem' — proof the fault is TLS, not the service. The app never ran. Case closed on the correct layer.

network-incident-runbook.caption: Run top-to-bottom; the first command that fails is your suspect layer. Paste its output into the packet as evidence.

network-incident-runbook.title: Two responses to the same partial outage
network-incident-runbook.subtitle: Both teams are busy. Only one is inspectable — and correct.

Rolls back the app, re-reads app logs
No dig, no openssl, no policy check
No constraint, no rejected option stated

Traced DNS → route → TLS; TLS verify code 21
openssl + curl output attached as evidence
Fix: reissue cert with correct SAN; rollback rejected (would mask it)
Invalidates-if: openssl verifies OK on a failing client

network-incident-runbook.caption: The gold packet names the layer before the fix, and says what result would prove it wrong.

network-incident-runbook.text: The senior tell is the invalidation line. 'Some clients, not others' plus a stated invalidation condition — 'if openssl verifies cleanly on a failing client, my TLS theory is dead' — is what separates a proven runbook from a plausible story. Distinguish stale from lost, and reachable-for-some from down: those words set the incident's urgency.

network-incident-runbook.question: A reviewer challenges your incident packet: 'You proved the fix worked — but did you prove the network was the cause and not the app?' What single piece of evidence answers this best?
options: The service returned 200 after you redeployed the application.
openssl s_client output showing Verify return code 21 and a stale SAN captured BEFORE any app change, from a failing client.
A screenshot of the dashboard turning green.
The app logs had no errors during the incident.
network-incident-runbook.explanation: The openssl output isolates the layer: it shows the TLS handshake failing on a failing client before HTTP or app code is reached, so the cause is certificate trust, not the application. A 200 after redeploy (0) and a green dashboard (2) prove the fix ran but not what the cause was — they are unfalsifiable. Quiet app logs (3) are consistent with the app never being the problem, but do not localize the fault the way layer-specific evidence does.

network-incident-runbook.intro: Prove your packet is a runbook, not a story:
items: You name the suspect LAYER (DNS / route+policy / TLS / HTTP) before you name the fix.
At least two inspection-hook outputs are pasted in — dig, kubectl describe networkpolicy, openssl s_client, or curl -v — from a failing client, not a healthy one.
The constraint table records what is observed vs inferred: 'subset of clients fail, post-deploy' is observed; 'stale SAN' is inferred until openssl confirms it.
You state the invalidation condition: the exact result that would kill your diagnosis.
The risk register names three residual risks (e.g. cert re-expiry, split-horizon DNS drift, policy applied to only some namespaces).

prompts: Trace the outage down the path out loud — DNS, route, TLS, HTTP — and say which layer lied and how you know.
Explain the blast radius using your own packet: which clients, how badly, and what stayed healthy (reachable-for-some ≠ down).
Defend the option you rejected: why does rolling back the app mask the real cause instead of fixing it?

network-incident-runbook.text: The move — trace the path, stop at the first layer that lies, prove it before you fix it — carries into any layered system. In a regulated enterprise, add change-control and a firewall-rule audit to the same packet; at high scale, the split-client signal appears as a per-region or per-AZ failure rate, and your first hooks become per-edge DNS and per-LB TLS checks. Same runbook, stricter environment. Your packet and its proof are exactly what the capstone incident replays.
